blocks.text: Every query you have written so far has looked at one table. That was never the real limit of SQL - it was the limit of the questions. Ask the KimTay bookkeeper what she needs on a Monday morning and it sounds like this: "Give me each customer with the name of the rep who handles them." Nothing in `CUSTOMER` stores a rep's name, and nothing in `REP` stores a customer's name. The answer lives in two tables at once.

That split is on purpose. Back in the design modules you saw why a rep's name is stored once in `REP` instead of being repeated on every customer row: one place to store it, one place to correct it. The price of that clean design is that answering a business question often means putting two tables back together for the length of one query. That is what a join does.
**Start with the data:** the first join uses `CUSTOMER` and `REP`. Read both complete source tables before seeing how SQL matches their `REP_NUM` values.

blocks.caption: Source table: CUSTOMER — all columns and all four rows
Source table: REP — all columns and all three rows

blocks.label: Join
blocks.text: A join combines rows from two tables by matching values in a column they share. `CUSTOMER.REP_NUM` and `REP.REP_NUM` hold the same kind of value, so a row in `CUSTOMER` and a row in `REP` belong together whenever those two values are equal.
5-1a Joining two tables

A join needs three things, and every one of them lives in a clause you already know. Nothing new is being added to the language here - you are widening the `FROM` clause and adding one more condition to `WHERE`.

items.title: 1. Name the columns you want, table and all
items.body: Write `CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME` rather than `CUSTOMER_NAME`. Qualifying a column with its table name is optional when the name appears in only one table, and required when it appears in both.

items.title: 2. List both tables in FROM
items.body: `FROM CUSTOMER, REP` tells the engine which two tables are in play. On its own this pairs every customer with every rep, which is not what you want yet.

items.title: 3. Write the matching condition in WHERE
items.body: `WHERE CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM` is the sentence that does the real work: keep a pairing only when the customer's rep number equals the rep's rep number.

blocks.text:
-- GOAL: list every customer next to the name of the rep who serves that account.
-- SELECT: the four columns the answer will contain. Each one is written as
--   TABLE.COLUMN, so it is plain that two values are read out of CUSTOMER and
--   two out of REP.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, REP.LAST_NAME, REP.FIRST_NAME

-- FROM: puts both tables in play. On its own this line pairs every customer with
--   every rep - 4 customers x 3 reps = 12 pairings, most of them nonsense.
FROM CUSTOMER, REP

-- WHERE: the matching condition, and the line that turns those 12 pairings into
--   a join. A pairing survives only when the rep number stored on the customer
--   row equals the rep number on the rep row, which leaves 4 real rows.
WHERE CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM

-- ORDER BY: sorts the surviving rows by customer number. It decides the order
--   rows are printed in, never which rows match.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM;

The `ORDER BY` on the end is not part of the join - the three parts above are the whole of it. It is there because a query without `ORDER BY` makes no promise about the sequence rows come back in, and every result printed in this module is easier to check against your own screen when the order is pinned down.

blocks.caption: Result: four customers, each carrying its rep's name

blocks.text: Read one row and the mechanism stops being mysterious. Customer 1120 stores `REP_NUM` 20. The engine looks for the row in `REP` whose `REP_NUM` is also 20, finds Valerie Kaiser, and glues the two rows together for output. Customer 1310 stores 20 as well, so Kaiser appears twice. Four customers in, four rows out - because every customer stores a rep number that matches exactly one rep, this join neither invents rows nor loses any.

blocks.label: Qualify anything that lives in both tables
blocks.text: `REP_NUM` exists in `CUSTOMER` and in `REP`, so writing it bare makes the request impossible to interpret. `SELECT REP_NUM FROM CUSTOMER, REP WHERE CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM;` fails with `ambiguous column name: REP_NUM`. That error message is telling you exactly what to fix: put a table name in front of it. `CUSTOMER_NAME` and `LAST_NAME` appear in only one table each, so those may be written bare - but qualifying every column in a join keeps the statement readable for whoever inherits it.

blocks.starter:
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME
FROM CUSTOMER, REP
WHERE CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.solution:
-- SELECT: four columns, two from each table, every one qualified as TABLE.COLUMN.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, REP.LAST_NAME, REP.FIRST_NAME
-- FROM: both tables in play. On its own this pairs every customer with every rep.
FROM CUSTOMER, REP
-- WHERE: the matching condition, and the line that makes this a join - keep a
-- pairing only when the two rep numbers agree.
WHERE CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM
-- ORDER BY: sorts the result; it never affects which rows match.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.hint: The starter already joins the two tables correctly - it is only selecting from one of them. Add `REP.LAST_NAME` and `REP.FIRST_NAME` to the column list. The row count does not change; the rows just get wider.

blocks.text: 5-1b Adding conditions to a join

The matching condition is a `WHERE` condition like any other, which means the compound conditions you learned in Module 4 still apply. Connect the matching condition to a business restriction with `AND`, and you get a filtered join. Here is every customer with a credit limit of 7500.00 or more, along with the rep who handles them.

-- GOAL: the same join, narrowed to customers with a credit limit of 7500 or more.
-- SELECT: three output columns - two read from CUSTOMER, one read from REP.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, REP.LAST_NAME

-- FROM: the two tables being joined.
FROM CUSTOMER, REP

-- WHERE: the matching condition - which customer row belongs with which rep row.
WHERE CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM

-- AND: an ordinary business restriction, exactly like the ones in Module 4.
--   Nothing about it is join-specific. Both conditions have to be true, so the
--   4 joined rows become the 2 whose credit limit clears 7500.
  AND CUSTOMER.CREDIT_LIMIT >= 7500

-- ORDER BY: sorts those two rows by customer number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM;

blocks.caption: Result: two high-limit customers, both handled by Kaiser

blocks.label: One condition per job
blocks.text: Keep the matching condition on its own line and the business restrictions underneath it. When a join returns something strange, the first line you check is the matching condition, and putting it first makes that a one-second check instead of a hunt.

blocks.starter:
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, REP.LAST_NAME
FROM CUSTOMER, REP
WHERE CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.solution:
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, REP.LAST_NAME
FROM CUSTOMER, REP
-- The matching condition: which customer row belongs with which rep row.
WHERE CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM
-- An ordinary business restriction on top of it. Both must be true, so the four
-- joined rows become the two whose credit limit clears 7500.
  AND CUSTOMER.CREDIT_LIMIT >= 7500
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.hint: Add one more line with `AND` under the matching condition, restricting `CUSTOMER.CREDIT_LIMIT`. Four rows should become two.

blocks.label: Leave out the matching condition and the row count explodes
blocks.text: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM CUSTOMER, REP;` returns 12. With no condition tying the tables together, the engine pairs each of the four customers with each of the three reps, and every one of those twelve pairings is reported as a row. Eight of them are nonsense - Access Pet Center paired with a rep who does not handle it. The special-operations section later in this module (5-5) gives this behavior its formal name; for now, treat a suspiciously large row count as a missing matching condition.

-- GOAL: show what the row count does when the matching condition is left out.
-- SELECT: COUNT(*) counts the rows this query produces, and AS gives that single
--   number the heading COMBINATIONS.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS COMBINATIONS

-- FROM: two tables and no WHERE clause anywhere, so nothing restricts the
--   pairings. Each of the 4 customers is paired with each of the 3 reps, and the
--   answer comes back 12 - eight rows more than the real join returned.
FROM CUSTOMER, REP;

Sorting, grouping and the aggregate functions do not change at all once a join is in the picture. The join produces rows; everything downstream treats those rows exactly like rows from a single table. This counts customers and totals balances per rep.

-- GOAL: one summary line per rep - how many customers, and their total balance.
-- SELECT: the grouping column first, then two aggregates. COUNT(*) counts the
--   rows inside each group, SUM adds up the balances inside each group, and AS
--   gives each computed value a readable heading.
SELECT REP.LAST_NAME, COUNT(*) AS NUM_CUSTOMERS, SUM(CUSTOMER.BALANCE) AS TOTAL_BALANCE

-- FROM: the two tables. Naming REP before CUSTOMER changes nothing - the order
--   of tables in FROM is cosmetic.
FROM REP, CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: the matching condition. It is applied BEFORE the grouping, so the
--   aggregates are computed over joined rows and never over the raw tables.
WHERE REP.REP_NUM = CUSTOMER.REP_NUM

-- GROUP BY: collapses the joined rows into one output row per rep last name.
--   Kaiser's two customers become a single line reading 2.
GROUP BY REP.LAST_NAME

-- ORDER BY: sorts those summary lines alphabetically by last name.
ORDER BY REP.LAST_NAME;

blocks.caption: Result: one row per rep

blocks.text: Kaiser's total is 3512.5 because her two customers carry balances of 3512.50 and 0.00. A balance of zero is a real, recorded amount - Companion Care Clinic is counted in `NUM_CUSTOMERS` like any other customer, and contributes nothing to the sum.

blocks.starter:
SELECT REP.LAST_NAME, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, CUSTOMER.BALANCE
FROM REP, CUSTOMER
WHERE REP.REP_NUM = CUSTOMER.REP_NUM
ORDER BY REP.LAST_NAME, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME;
blocks.solution:
-- The grouping column, then two aggregates over the joined rows.
SELECT REP.LAST_NAME, COUNT(*) AS NUM_CUSTOMERS, SUM(CUSTOMER.BALANCE) AS TOTAL_BALANCE
FROM REP, CUSTOMER
-- The matching condition is applied BEFORE the grouping, so the aggregates are
-- computed over joined rows rather than over either raw table.
WHERE REP.REP_NUM = CUSTOMER.REP_NUM
-- One output row per rep last name.
GROUP BY REP.LAST_NAME
ORDER BY REP.LAST_NAME;
blocks.hint: Start from the four detail rows, then collapse them: replace the customer columns with `COUNT(*)` and `SUM(CUSTOMER.BALANCE)`, and add `GROUP BY REP.LAST_NAME`. Four rows become three.

cards.title: What goes wrong
cards.body: Naming two tables in `FROM` and forgetting the matching condition. Writing a shared column name without its table. Assuming the order of the tables in `FROM` matters - it does not, `FROM CUSTOMER, REP` and `FROM REP, CUSTOMER` return the same rows.

cards.title: What to do instead
cards.body: Write `FROM` and the matching condition together as one habit, before you touch the column list. Qualify every column in a join. Run the join with no extra restrictions first, confirm the row count looks sane, and only then start filtering.

items: Both tables appear in the `FROM` clause, separated by a comma
A `WHERE` condition equates the matching columns from the two tables
Any column name that exists in both tables is written as `TABLE.COLUMN`
Extra business restrictions are joined to the matching condition with `AND`
The row count is what you expected - a surprising jump means the matching condition is missing
An `ORDER BY` is present whenever the order of the output matters to you

blocks.text: Here is a question the KimTay bookkeeper actually asks: which customers have placed at least one order? SQL will answer it three different ways - with a join, with `IN`, and with `EXISTS` - and all three return the same three customers. That is not wasted effort on the language's part. Each shape says something different about what you meant, and one of them will read better than the others depending on what you need in the output.

Keep one row in mind for this whole section: Companion Care Clinic, customer 1310. It is a real customer with a 10000.00 credit limit and no invoice at all. It is the row that tells you whether a query is answering "has an order" or something subtly different.
5-2a Using the IN operator
You already use `IN` with a list you type yourself. This asks for customers in either of two cities, and the engine checks the `CITY` value of each row against the two values in the parentheses.

-- GOAL: the customers located in either of two named cities.
-- SELECT: three columns. Only one table is involved, so nothing has to be
--   qualified with a table name.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, CITY

-- FROM: a single table - this query is not a join at all.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: IN is true when the row's CITY equals ANY value inside the parentheses.
--   It is shorthand for CITY = 'Maple Grove' OR CITY = 'Brookville', and the
--   longer the list, the more typing it saves.
WHERE CITY IN ('Maple Grove', 'Brookville')

-- ORDER BY: sorts the matching rows by customer number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

The step that makes `IN` powerful is realizing the list does not have to be typed. A subquery that returns a single column produces a list, and `IN` cannot tell the difference. Compare the two ways of answering the order question. First the join, using exactly the pattern from 5-1a.

-- GOAL: which customers have at least one invoice - answered with a join.
-- SELECT: DISTINCT throws away duplicate output rows. It is here because a join
--   returns one row per matching PAIR, so a customer holding three invoices
--   would otherwise be listed three times.
SELECT DISTINCT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: the customer table and the invoice table.
FROM CUSTOMER, INVOICE

-- WHERE: the matching condition, written on the customer number the two tables
--   share. A customer with no invoice matches nothing here and disappears from
--   the result - which is exactly what "has at least one invoice" means.
WHERE CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM = INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM

-- ORDER BY: sorts the surviving customers by number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM;
Now the same question with `IN`. The inner query returns the customer numbers that appear in `INVOICE`; the outer query keeps the customers whose number is in that list.

-- GOAL: the same question - customers with at least one invoice - written with a
-- subquery instead of a join.
-- SELECT: two columns, both from CUSTOMER. No DISTINCT is needed this time.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: one table only. INVOICE is reached by the subquery below, not by FROM.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: the inner SELECT runs first, on its own, and returns a one-column list
--   of the customer numbers that appear in INVOICE. IN then tests each customer
--   once against that finished list, which is why no customer can come back
--   twice and why DISTINCT is unnecessary.
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM IN (SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM FROM INVOICE)

-- ORDER BY: sorts the kept customers by number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

blocks.caption: Both statements return the same three customers

blocks.label: Why the join needed DISTINCT
blocks.text: A join returns one row per matching pair, so a customer with three invoices comes back three times. In the shipped data every customer that has an invoice at all happens to have exactly one - Companion Care Clinic has none - so this particular join returns three rows even without `DISTINCT`. That is an accident of this small data set, not a rule. Write `DISTINCT` whenever a join is being used to answer a "which rows have at least one match" question. `IN` needs no such defense: the outer query still looks at each customer exactly once.
The duplicate problem is visible in the shipped data if you join `ITEM` to `INVOICE_LINE` instead. Item CF21 was ordered on two different invoices, so the join reports it twice.

-- GOAL: show which invoices ordered each item, so the duplicate rows a join can
-- produce are visible in the shipped data.
-- SELECT: two columns from ITEM and one from INVOICE_LINE. There is deliberately
--   no DISTINCT here, because the repeats are the point of the example.
SELECT ITEM.ITEM_ID, ITEM.DESCRIPTION, INVOICE_LINE.INVOICE_NUM

-- FROM: the item table plus the line-item table that records what was ordered.
FROM ITEM, INVOICE_LINE

-- WHERE: the matching condition on the item id the two tables share. Item CF21
--   was ordered on two different invoices, so CF21 makes two matching pairs -
--   and a join reports one row per pair. Five items, six rows.
WHERE ITEM.ITEM_ID = INVOICE_LINE.ITEM_ID

-- ORDER BY: two sort columns - by item first, then by invoice within each item.
ORDER BY ITEM.ITEM_ID, INVOICE_LINE.INVOICE_NUM;

blocks.caption: Six rows for five items - CF21 appears on two invoices

blocks.label: The rule of thumb for IN
blocks.text: If the output shows columns from one table only, `IN` is usually the cleaner statement. If the output has to show columns from both tables - the invoice number next to the customer name, the description next to the quantity - a join is the only one of the three that can do it, because a subquery's columns never reach the output.

blocks.starter:
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM IN (SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM FROM INVOICE)
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.solution:
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME
FROM CUSTOMER
-- The inner SELECT runs first and returns a list of customer numbers. IN then
-- tests each customer once against that list, so no duplicate can appear and
-- DISTINCT is unnecessary.
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM IN (SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM FROM INVOICE)
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

-- The same shape aimed at a different question: which items are on invoice 50710.
SELECT ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION, PRICE
FROM ITEM
-- Run the inner query alone first and you get CF21 and DG04 - the list IN tests against.
WHERE ITEM_ID IN
    (SELECT ITEM_ID FROM INVOICE_LINE WHERE INVOICE_NUM = '50710')
ORDER BY ITEM_ID;
blocks.hint: Your task: leave the starter alone and write a second statement below it that lists the ITEM_ID, DESCRIPTION and PRICE of every item ordered on invoice 50710, using the same `IN` shape. Run the inner query by itself first - `SELECT ITEM_ID FROM INVOICE_LINE WHERE INVOICE_NUM = '50710';` returns CF21 and DG04. Those two values are the list the outer query checks against, so expect two rows.

blocks.text: 5-2b Using the EXISTS operator

`EXISTS` asks a yes-or-no question about the row currently being examined: is there at least one row over in that other table that matches me? It does not produce values, and nothing from inside it reaches the output. It returns true or false, and the outer `WHERE` keeps the row or drops it.

-- GOAL: customers with at least one invoice - the third way, using EXISTS.
-- SELECT: the two columns to print. Nothing from inside the subquery can ever
--   appear in this list.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: the outer query walks CUSTOMER one row at a time.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: EXISTS is a yes-or-no test applied to the customer currently being
--   examined - did the inner query find at least one row? It answers true or
--   false and produces no values of its own.
WHERE EXISTS

    -- SELECT *: the column list is irrelevant, since no value from it is used.
    --   The * reads as "anything at all", which is the question EXISTS asks.
    (SELECT *

     -- FROM: the table being searched for a match.
     FROM INVOICE

     -- WHERE: this line names CUSTOMER, a table of the OUTER query, and that
     --   reference is what makes the subquery correlated: it cannot run on its
     --   own, and it is re-executed for each customer with that customer's
     --   number filled in. Customer 1310 finds no invoice, so EXISTS is false
     --   and that row is dropped.
     WHERE INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM = CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM)

-- ORDER BY: sorts the three kept customers by number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

blocks.label: Correlated subquery
blocks.text: Look at the inner `WHERE`: it mentions `CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM`, a column of the outer query. That reference is what makes the subquery correlated - it cannot be run on its own, because it has no meaning until the outer query hands it a customer. An `IN` subquery is the opposite: `SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM FROM INVOICE` runs perfectly well by itself.

items.title: Customer 1120, Access Pet Center
items.body: The inner query becomes "is there an invoice whose `CUSTOMER_NUM` is 1120?" Invoice 50710 matches. The engine stops looking the moment it finds that first row - it never needs to know how many there are. True, so the row is kept.

items.title: Customer 1225, Downtown Aquarium & Pets
items.body: Invoice 50712 matches. True, kept.

items.title: Customer 1310, Companion Care Clinic
items.body: The inner query searches `INVOICE` for `CUSTOMER_NUM` 1310 and finds nothing. False, so the row is dropped. This is the one customer the query removes.

items.title: Customer 1420, Whiskers & Wags Boutique
items.body: Invoice 50711 matches. True, kept. Three rows come back, the same three the join and the `IN` version returned.

blocks.text: Writing `SELECT *` inside `EXISTS` is the convention, and it is not laziness. Since no value from the subquery is ever used, the column list is irrelevant - `SELECT 1` returns the identical three customers. `SELECT *` reads as "anything at all," which is precisely the question being asked.

blocks.label: An EXISTS with no correlation is always true
blocks.text: Drop the inner `WHERE` and you get `SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM INVOICE);` - which returns all four customers, Companion Care Clinic included. The subquery no longer asks about a particular customer; it asks whether `INVOICE` has any rows at all, and it does. If an `EXISTS` query returns every row of the outer table, the correlation is missing.

Reverse the test and `EXISTS` earns its keep. `NOT EXISTS` finds the rows where the search comes back empty - the customers who have never been invoiced. There is exactly one, and by now you know which.

-- GOAL: the opposite question - which customers have never been invoiced.
-- SELECT: the two columns to print.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: the outer query walks CUSTOMER one row at a time, as before.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: NOT EXISTS flips the test. The customer is kept only when the inner
--   query finds NOTHING. This is the standard pattern for finding rows that have
--   no match at all on the other side.
WHERE NOT EXISTS

    -- SELECT *: again the column list does not matter; only whether a row exists.
    (SELECT *

     -- FROM: the table searched for a match.
     FROM INVOICE

     -- WHERE: the correlation back to the outer row. For each customer in turn
     --   the engine asks "is there an invoice carrying this customer number?"
     --   Only 1310 comes back empty, so only 1310 survives NOT EXISTS.
     WHERE INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM = CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM)

-- ORDER BY: sorts the result, which here is a single row.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

blocks.caption: Result: the customer with no invoice

blocks.text: This is the shape a join cannot express with what you know so far. A join reports pairs that matched, so a customer with no invoice produces no row and disappears from the output entirely - you cannot see an absence in a list of matches. The special-operations section later in this module (5-5) introduces a kind of join built for exactly this, but `NOT EXISTS` answers it today.

blocks.caption: Picking a shape
rows: Columns from both tables side by side
Only a join puts values from two tables on one output row
Columns from one table, filtered by another
The inner query is an independent list of values to match against
One table, keeping rows that have a match
A yes-or-no test that stops at the first matching row
One table, keeping rows that have no match
States the absence directly instead of hunting for it

blocks.starter:
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME
FROM CUSTOMER
WHERE EXISTS
    (SELECT *
     FROM INVOICE
     WHERE INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM = CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM)
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.solution:
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME
FROM CUSTOMER
-- EXISTS is a yes-or-no test on the customer being examined: did the inner query
-- find at least one row? It returns true or false and no values of its own.
WHERE EXISTS
    -- SELECT * because the column list is irrelevant - only whether a row exists.
    (SELECT *
     FROM INVOICE
     -- Naming CUSTOMER here makes the subquery correlated: it is re-run once per
     -- customer, with that customer's number filled in.
     WHERE INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM = CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM)
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

-- The same query with the test reversed.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME
FROM CUSTOMER
-- NOT EXISTS keeps the customer only when the inner query finds NOTHING. This is
-- the standard pattern for finding rows with no match on the other side.
WHERE NOT EXISTS
    (SELECT *
     FROM INVOICE
     WHERE INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM = CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM)
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.hint: Run the `EXISTS` version as given, then copy it underneath and add `NOT` in front of `EXISTS` in the copy. Three rows from the first, one from the second - between them the two statements account for all four customers.

blocks.text: 5-2c Using a subquery within a subquery

Some questions travel further than one table away. "Which customers have ordered the Grain-Free Dry Food?" starts at an item and ends at a customer, and the path runs `ITEM` to `INVOICE_LINE` to `INVOICE` to `CUSTOMER`. You do not need a new construct for that - you need the same `IN` subquery, nested inside itself. Build it from the inside out and run each layer as you go.

items.title: Innermost: which invoices contain item CF21?
items.body: `SELECT INVOICE_NUM FROM INVOICE_LINE WHERE ITEM_ID = 'CF21';` returns 50710 and 50711. Run this first and you have a list of invoice numbers you can check by eye.

items.title: Middle: which customers own those invoices?
items.body: Wrap the first query in a query over `INVOICE`. `SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM FROM INVOICE WHERE INVOICE_NUM IN (...)` returns 1120 and 1420.

items.title: Outer: what are those customers called?
items.body: Wrap that in a query over `CUSTOMER`. `SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM IN (...)` turns the two numbers into two names.

blocks.text:
-- GOAL: which customers ordered item CF21? The path runs INVOICE_LINE to INVOICE
-- to CUSTOMER, so one IN subquery is nested inside another. SQL evaluates them
-- from the inside out, and so should you when reading.
-- SELECT: the two columns printed at the end. Only CUSTOMER columns are output;
--   the subqueries supply values for testing, never for display.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: the outer query reads CUSTOMER.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: step 3, the last test to run. Keep a customer whose number appears in
--   the list the middle subquery returns (1120 and 1420).
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM IN

    -- SELECT: step 2 returns one column, the customer number on each matching
    --   invoice. This is the list the outer IN tests against.
    (SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM

     -- FROM: the middle query reads INVOICE.
     FROM INVOICE

     -- WHERE: keep an invoice whose number is in the list step 1 returns.
     WHERE INVOICE_NUM IN

         -- SELECT: step 1, the innermost query, runs FIRST. It returns the
         --   invoice numbers that contain item CF21: 50710 and 50711.
         (SELECT INVOICE_NUM

          -- FROM: the innermost query reads the line-item table.
          FROM INVOICE_LINE

          -- WHERE: the only literal value in the whole statement. Both closing
          --   parentheses land here, one for each subquery being closed.
          WHERE ITEM_ID = 'CF21'))

-- ORDER BY: sorts the two customers that survive.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

blocks.label: Read nested queries from the inside out
blocks.text: The engine evaluates the innermost query first, then the one containing it, then the outer query. That is also the order in which you should write and test them. Three nested queries typed all at once and run for the first time is three places for a mistake to hide; three queries run one at a time is three confirmations.

The indentation is doing real work here. Each subquery sits one level deeper than the one that contains it, and every open parenthesis has a visible partner. When a nested query will not run, an unbalanced parenthesis is the first thing to count.

blocks.solution:
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME
FROM CUSTOMER
-- Step 3, the last test to run: keep customers whose number is in the middle list.
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM IN
    -- Step 2: the customer number on each matching invoice.
    (SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM
     FROM INVOICE
     WHERE INVOICE_NUM IN
         -- Step 1 runs FIRST: the invoices that contain item CF21.
         (SELECT INVOICE_NUM
          FROM INVOICE_LINE
          -- Both closing parentheses land here, one per subquery.
          WHERE ITEM_ID = 'CF21'))
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.hint: The starter is the innermost layer, and it returns 50710 and 50711. Wrap it in the `INVOICE` query and run that - two customer numbers. Then wrap that in the `CUSTOMER` query. Two rows at the end.

blocks.text: 5-2d A comprehensive example

Time to put it together. The request: an order detail report for the customers handled by the reps working out of Maple Grove. Every line should show the customer name, the invoice number, what was ordered, and what that line came to. Four tables, a computed column, and a subquery - and none of it is new. Build it in stages and run each stage.

items.title: Stage 1 - turn item IDs into words
items.body: `INVOICE_LINE` stores `ITEM_ID`, which nobody wants to read. Join it to `ITEM` on `ITEM_ID` to get the description. Six rows, one per invoice line.

items.title: Stage 2 - attach the invoice and the customer
items.body: Add `INVOICE` and `CUSTOMER` to `FROM` and add their matching conditions. Three tables means two matching conditions; four tables means three. Still six rows - a chain of matching conditions along foreign keys does not change the count.

items.title: Stage 3 - compute the line total
items.body: `NUM_ORDERED * QUOTED_PRICE` is a computed column of the kind you met in Module 4. Give it a name with `AS` so the heading reads `LINE_TOTAL` instead of the arithmetic.

items.title: Stage 4 - restrict to the Maple Grove reps
items.body: The report is not for every rep. `CUSTOMER.REP_NUM IN (SELECT REP_NUM FROM REP WHERE CITY = 'Maple Grove')` cuts it to the customers of reps 20 and 35, and the six rows become four.

blocks.text:
-- GOAL: stage 1 of the order detail report - put a readable description on every
-- invoice line, instead of the item id the line actually stores.
-- SELECT: the invoice number and quantity come from INVOICE_LINE; the wording of
--   the item comes from ITEM.
SELECT INVOICE_LINE.INVOICE_NUM, ITEM.DESCRIPTION, INVOICE_LINE.NUM_ORDERED

-- FROM: two tables, so exactly one matching condition will be needed.
FROM INVOICE_LINE, ITEM

-- WHERE: the matching condition on the shared item id. Because every line item
--   points at a real item, the six line items come back as six rows - a join
--   along a foreign key neither invents rows nor loses any.
WHERE INVOICE_LINE.ITEM_ID = ITEM.ITEM_ID

-- ORDER BY: by invoice, then by description within each invoice.
ORDER BY INVOICE_LINE.INVOICE_NUM, ITEM.DESCRIPTION;

-- GOAL: stage 2 - carry the customer and the invoice date onto every line. Four
-- tables in FROM means three matching conditions, one per link in the chain
-- CUSTOMER to INVOICE to INVOICE_LINE to ITEM.
-- SELECT: five columns drawn from four different tables. This is the reason a
--   join is unavoidable here - a subquery could not put them side by side.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM, INVOICE.INVOICE_DATE,

-- SELECT (continued): the column list simply wraps onto a second line; SQL does
--   not care where the line breaks fall, only where the commas are.
       ITEM.DESCRIPTION, INVOICE_LINE.NUM_ORDERED

-- FROM: all four tables. Count them, then count the conditions below: four
--   tables always need three links, and one link short makes the count explode.
FROM CUSTOMER, INVOICE, INVOICE_LINE, ITEM

-- WHERE: link 1 - ties each customer to the invoices belonging to it.
WHERE CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM = INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM

-- AND: link 2 - ties each invoice to its own line items.
  AND INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM = INVOICE_LINE.INVOICE_NUM

-- AND: link 3 - ties each line item to the item it refers to. Still six rows,
--   because following foreign keys does not change the number of lines.
  AND INVOICE_LINE.ITEM_ID = ITEM.ITEM_ID

-- ORDER BY: by invoice, then by description within each invoice.
ORDER BY INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM, ITEM.DESCRIPTION;

-- GOAL: stage 3 - the same four-table join, with the money worked out per line.
-- SELECT: three plain columns first, one from each of three tables.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM, ITEM.DESCRIPTION,

-- SELECT (continued): a calculated column. The multiplication is performed once
--   for each row, and AS names the result so the heading reads LINE_TOTAL rather
--   than the arithmetic itself. Nothing is stored - it exists in the output only.
       INVOICE_LINE.NUM_ORDERED * INVOICE_LINE.QUOTED_PRICE AS LINE_TOTAL

-- FROM: the same four tables as before.
FROM CUSTOMER, INVOICE, INVOICE_LINE, ITEM

-- WHERE: link 1 - customer to invoice.
WHERE CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM = INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM

-- AND: link 2 - invoice to line item.
  AND INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM = INVOICE_LINE.INVOICE_NUM

-- AND: link 3 - line item to item.
  AND INVOICE_LINE.ITEM_ID = ITEM.ITEM_ID

-- ORDER BY: by invoice, then by description.
ORDER BY INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM, ITEM.DESCRIPTION;

-- GOAL: stage 4 - the finished report, restricted to the customers whose rep
-- works out of Maple Grove. Note that the restriction is about reps, yet no rep
-- column appears in the output: that is the situation a subquery is made for.
-- SELECT: the three display columns.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM, ITEM.DESCRIPTION,

-- SELECT (continued): the calculated line total, named with AS.
       INVOICE_LINE.NUM_ORDERED * INVOICE_LINE.QUOTED_PRICE AS LINE_TOTAL

-- FROM: the four tables the output columns come from.
FROM CUSTOMER, INVOICE, INVOICE_LINE, ITEM

-- WHERE: link 1 - customer to invoice.
WHERE CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM = INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM

-- AND: link 2 - invoice to line item.
  AND INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM = INVOICE_LINE.INVOICE_NUM

-- AND: link 3 - line item to item.
  AND INVOICE_LINE.ITEM_ID = ITEM.ITEM_ID

-- AND: NOT a link - this is the business restriction. The subquery returns the
--   numbers of the reps based in Maple Grove (20 and 35), and IN keeps only the
--   customers whose REP_NUM appears in that list. Six rows become four.
  AND CUSTOMER.REP_NUM IN

-- The subquery reads CITY from REP, not from CUSTOMER. Downtown Aquarium is in
-- Northfield and still qualifies, because its rep is in Maple Grove.
      (SELECT REP_NUM FROM REP WHERE CITY = 'Maple Grove')

-- ORDER BY: by invoice, then by description.
ORDER BY INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM, ITEM.DESCRIPTION;

blocks.caption: Final result: four order lines for the Maple Grove reps' customers

blocks.label: Whose city is being tested
blocks.text: The subquery reads `CITY` from `REP`, not from `CUSTOMER`, and the two are easy to confuse. Downtown Aquarium & Pets is in Northfield, yet it appears in the report, because its rep - Hull, number 35 - works out of Maple Grove. Companion Care Clinic is in Maple Grove and is handled by a Maple Grove rep, yet it does not appear, because it has no invoice and therefore no order lines to report. Read a restriction back as a sentence before you trust it.

Notice what each piece contributed. The join is there because the output needs a column from all four tables at once. The subquery is there because the restriction is about reps, and no rep column appears in the output. Neither could have done the other's job.

blocks.label: Counting the matching conditions
blocks.text: Four tables in `FROM` need three matching conditions - one for each link in the chain `CUSTOMER` to `INVOICE` to `INVOICE_LINE` to `ITEM`. One condition short of that and the row count jumps sharply, because the unlinked table gets paired with everything. Counting conditions against tables is the fastest check on a multi-table query: conditions equals tables minus one.

blocks.starter:
SELECT INVOICE_LINE.INVOICE_NUM, ITEM.DESCRIPTION, INVOICE_LINE.NUM_ORDERED
FROM INVOICE_LINE, ITEM
WHERE INVOICE_LINE.ITEM_ID = ITEM.ITEM_ID
ORDER BY INVOICE_LINE.INVOICE_NUM, ITEM.DESCRIPTION;
blocks.solution:
-- Three display columns drawn from three different tables...
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM, ITEM.DESCRIPTION,
-- ...plus a calculated one. The multiplication runs once per row; AS names it.
       INVOICE_LINE.NUM_ORDERED * INVOICE_LINE.QUOTED_PRICE AS LINE_TOTAL
-- Four tables in FROM always need three matching conditions.
FROM CUSTOMER, INVOICE, INVOICE_LINE, ITEM
-- Link 1: customer to invoice.
WHERE CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM = INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM
-- Link 2: invoice to line item.
  AND INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM = INVOICE_LINE.INVOICE_NUM
-- Link 3: line item to item.
  AND INVOICE_LINE.ITEM_ID = ITEM.ITEM_ID
-- NOT a link - the business restriction. The subquery returns the Maple Grove
-- reps, and IN keeps only the customers those reps serve.
  AND CUSTOMER.REP_NUM IN
      -- Note whose city is tested: the REP's, not the customer's.
      (SELECT REP_NUM FROM REP WHERE CITY = 'Maple Grove')
ORDER BY INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM, ITEM.DESCRIPTION;
blocks.hint: Work up one stage at a time and run after each. Six rows through stage 3, four rows once the `IN` restriction goes on.

blocks.text: One more turn of the same crank, to show that everything from Module 4 is still available. Group the lines by invoice and the detail report becomes an invoice summary. Only three tables are needed now, because no item description appears in the output - so two matching conditions, not three.

-- GOAL: turn the detail report into a summary - one total per invoice. Only three
-- tables are needed now, because no item description appears in the output, so
-- there are two matching conditions rather than three.
-- SELECT: the two columns that identify each group.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM,

-- SELECT (continued): the same multiplication as before, wrapped in SUM so the
--   line totals inside one group are added into a single invoice total.
       SUM(INVOICE_LINE.NUM_ORDERED * INVOICE_LINE.QUOTED_PRICE) AS INVOICE_TOTAL

-- FROM: three tables, so two links.
FROM CUSTOMER, INVOICE, INVOICE_LINE

-- WHERE: link 1 - customer to invoice.
WHERE CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM = INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM

-- AND: link 2 - invoice to line item. Both links are applied before grouping.
  AND INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM = INVOICE_LINE.INVOICE_NUM

-- GROUP BY: collapses the six joined rows into one row per invoice. Every column
--   in SELECT that is not inside an aggregate has to be listed here, which is
--   why CUSTOMER_NAME appears as well as INVOICE_NUM.
GROUP BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM

-- ORDER BY: sorts the three summary rows by invoice number.
ORDER BY INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM;

blocks.caption: Result: one row per invoice

items: Output needs columns from two tables at once - use a join, and remember `DISTINCT` if you only want the matched rows listed once
Output needs one table, filtered by values sitting in another - use `IN` with a subquery
Output needs one table, and the test is "does a match exist" - use `EXISTS`, and make sure the inner query names an outer column
Output needs the rows with no match anywhere - use `NOT EXISTS`
The question spans three or more tables - nest the subqueries, and run each layer before you wrap the next one around it
The number of matching conditions equals the number of tables minus one
An `IN` subquery returns exactly one column
An `EXISTS` subquery mentions a column of the outer query in its `WHERE` clause
A join used to find "has at least one match" is protected with `DISTINCT`
Every nested query was run on its own before it was wrapped in the next layer
A restriction naming a column such as `CITY` was checked against the table it actually reads from
Companion Care Clinic appears when the question is about absence, and not when it is about orders

questions.scenarioTitle: Putting a rep's name next to a customer
questions.stem: The KimTay bookkeeper needs a list showing each customer name with the last name of the rep who handles that customer. She has written `SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, REP.LAST_NAME FROM CUSTOMER, REP` and stopped. What has to come next for the names to line up correctly?
options: Listing both tables in the FROM clause is enough, because SQL pairs the rows in order
A WHERE condition equating CUSTOMER.REP_NUM to REP.REP_NUM, so each customer keeps only its own rep
An ORDER BY on REP.LAST_NAME, which gathers each customer underneath the rep who handles it
A DISTINCT in front of the column list, which removes the pairings that do not belong together
optionNotes: Naming two tables only makes both available; with no condition the engine pairs every customer with every rep, giving twelve rows.
Right - the matching condition on the shared REP_NUM value is what turns twelve possible pairings into the four correct ones.
ORDER BY changes the sequence rows are displayed in and never removes or corrects a wrong pairing.
DISTINCT removes duplicate rows, but the twelve pairings here are all different from one another, so none of them would be dropped.
questions.takeaway: A join is two tables in FROM plus a WHERE condition equating the columns they share - the condition, not the FROM clause, is what matches the rows.

questions.scenarioTitle: The twelve-row surprise at KimTay Pet Supplies
questions.stem: Someone runs `SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, REP.LAST_NAME FROM CUSTOMER, REP;` against the KimTay database and gets twelve rows, even though there are only four customers. What happened?
options: The CUSTOMER table holds twelve rows, and the earlier single-table queries were hiding eight of them
The engine repeated the output three times because three columns were involved in the statement
The REP_NUM values failed to match, so the engine padded the result with eight empty rows
With no matching condition every customer was paired with every rep, and four times three is twelve
optionNotes: CUSTOMER has four rows; nothing was hidden, and a SELECT with no WHERE clause never conceals rows.
Row counts come from how rows are combined, not from how many columns appear in the SELECT list.
No padding takes place - each of the twelve rows holds a real customer and a real rep, they are merely paired wrongly.
Right - without a matching condition the engine reports every possible pairing, four customers times three reps.
questions.takeaway: A row count far larger than either table is the signature of a missing matching condition in the WHERE clause.

questions.scenarioTitle: The message that stopped the query
questions.stem: A student runs `SELECT REP_NUM FROM CUSTOMER, REP WHERE CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM;` and the engine answers `ambiguous column name: REP_NUM`. What is the engine complaining about?
options: REP_NUM exists in both tables, so the SELECT list must say CUSTOMER.REP_NUM or REP.REP_NUM
REP_NUM is misspelled somewhere in the statement, and the engine cannot locate the column
Only one table may be named in FROM when the SELECT list contains a primary key column
REP_NUM has already been used in the WHERE clause, so it cannot appear in the SELECT list too
optionNotes: Right - a column name that appears in more than one table has to be qualified so the engine knows which table you mean.
The spelling is correct in all three places; the engine found the column in two tables, which is the actual problem.
There is no such restriction - a join may select any column from any table listed in FROM.
A column may appear in both the WHERE clause and the SELECT list as often as you need it.
questions.takeaway: Ambiguous column name means the column lives in more than one table in your FROM clause - qualify it as TABLE.COLUMN.

questions.scenarioTitle: The rep with two customers
questions.stem: The grouped query `SELECT REP.LAST_NAME, COUNT(*) AS NUM_CUSTOMERS, SUM(CUSTOMER.BALANCE) AS TOTAL_BALANCE FROM REP, CUSTOMER WHERE REP.REP_NUM = CUSTOMER.REP_NUM GROUP BY REP.LAST_NAME;` reports Kaiser with NUM_CUSTOMERS of 2 and TOTAL_BALANCE of 3512.5, even though Kaiser handles Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic. Why does the total match a single customer's balance?
options: Companion Care Clinic was dropped from the join, so only one of Kaiser's customers reached the SUM
Companion Care Clinic has a recorded balance of 0.00, so it is counted but adds nothing to the total
SUM ignores the second row of every group and totals only the first one it encounters
COUNT and SUM were computed over different groups, so their numbers are not comparable
optionNotes: It was not dropped - it stores REP_NUM 20 and matches Kaiser, which is exactly why NUM_CUSTOMERS reports 2.
Right - a balance of 0.00 is a real recorded amount, so the row is counted by COUNT(*) and contributes zero to the SUM.
SUM adds every value in the group; there is no rule that skips rows after the first.
Both are computed over the same group, which is why the count of 2 and the total of 3512.5 sit on one row together.
questions.takeaway: A zero is a value, not a missing row - it is counted like any other row and simply adds nothing to a total.

quizzes.heading: Knowledge check: joins, IN, and EXISTS

questions.scenarioTitle: Which pet stores have ordered from KimTay
questions.stem: The bookkeeper wants a list of customer numbers and names for the customers that appear on at least one invoice. No invoice number, date, or amount belongs on the printout. Which shape fits the request most cleanly?
options: A join of CUSTOMER and INVOICE, because any question touching two tables has to be a join
Two separate queries run one after the other, then compared by eye on the two printouts
IN with a subquery returning INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM, because only CUSTOMER columns reach the output
EXISTS with an inner query that leaves out the WHERE clause, so it checks the whole INVOICE table
optionNotes: A join would work but needs DISTINCT to stay honest once a customer has several invoices, so it is the noisier choice here.
Comparing two printouts by hand is not a query, and it stops being possible the moment the tables grow.
Right - the output is CUSTOMER columns only, so an independent list of invoiced customer numbers is all the outer query needs.
An EXISTS with no reference to the outer row is true for every customer, so it would return Companion Care Clinic as well.
questions.takeaway: When the output shows columns from one table only, IN with a subquery says what you mean with the least machinery.

questions.scenarioTitle: The EXISTS that returned every customer
questions.stem: A query written as `SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM INVOICE);` returns all four KimTay customers, including Companion Care Clinic, which has never been invoiced. Why?
options: The inner query never mentions the outer customer, so it is true for every row that gets tested
SELECT * inside EXISTS returns every column of INVOICE, which forces the outer query to keep every row
Companion Care Clinic has a balance of 0.00, and EXISTS treats a zero balance as a match
The inner query needs DISTINCT, otherwise duplicate invoice rows multiply the rows of the outer query
optionNotes: Right - the subquery asks only whether INVOICE has any rows at all, which is true no matter which customer is being tested.
The column list inside EXISTS is ignored entirely; SELECT * and SELECT 1 behave identically.
Balance plays no part - the subquery never looks at CUSTOMER.BALANCE, and EXISTS tests only for the presence of a row.
EXISTS stops at the first matching row, so duplicates in the inner query cannot multiply anything.
questions.takeaway: An EXISTS subquery must reference a column of the outer query, or it becomes a single true-or-false answer applied to every row.

questions.scenarioTitle: Who bought the Grain-Free Dry Food
questions.stem: To find the customers who ordered item CF21, a query nests an INVOICE_LINE subquery inside an INVOICE subquery inside a query on CUSTOMER. In what order does the engine work through the three levels?
options: The outer CUSTOMER query runs first and passes its rows down into the two inner queries
All three run at the same moment, and the engine keeps whichever result finishes first
The middle INVOICE query runs first, because INVOICE sits between the other two tables
The innermost INVOICE_LINE query runs first, and each result becomes the list for the query above it
optionNotes: That describes a correlated subquery such as EXISTS; an IN subquery is independent and does not receive outer rows.
SQL evaluates nested queries in a defined order, and results are never chosen by which one finishes first.
Position in the diagram does not set the order - nesting does, and INVOICE_LINE is nested deepest.
Right - the deepest query produces invoice numbers 50710 and 50711, which the INVOICE query turns into customer numbers 1120 and 1420.
questions.takeaway: Nested subqueries evaluate from the inside out, which is also the safest order to write and test them in.

questions.scenarioTitle: The order detail report
questions.stem: The report must print the customer name, the invoice number, the item description, and the quantity multiplied by the quoted price, one line per invoice line. Which shape can produce it?
options: EXISTS against INVOICE_LINE, since the report needs to confirm that invoice lines are present
A join across CUSTOMER, INVOICE, INVOICE_LINE and ITEM, because output columns come from all four
IN with a subquery on INVOICE_LINE, because a subquery can supply the description to the outer query
Four single-table queries printed side by side and lined up by their row numbers on the page
optionNotes: EXISTS returns true or false and contributes no columns, so it cannot put a description on the printout.
Right - only a join can place values from four different tables on one output row, which is what the report is.
A subquery's columns never reach the output; IN uses them to test a value and then discards them.
Row order is not a relationship - lining up separate printouts by position invents pairings the data does not support.
questions.takeaway: The moment the output needs columns from more than one table, the answer is a join, whatever else the query also does.

questions.scenarioTitle: Reading the Maple Grove restriction
questions.stem: The comprehensive report restricts rows with `CUSTOMER.REP_NUM IN (SELECT REP_NUM FROM REP WHERE CITY = 'Maple Grove')`. Downtown Aquarium & Pets is located in Northfield, yet its invoice lines appear on the report. Is the query wrong?
options: Yes - the subquery should read CUSTOMER.CITY, because the report is about where customers are located
No - CITY is read from REP, and Downtown Aquarium & Pets is handled by Hull, who works out of Maple Grove
Yes - Northfield rows should have been removed, so a matching condition must be missing from the WHERE clause
No - IN ignores the city entirely and simply returns every rep number stored in the REP table
optionNotes: The request asked for the customers of the Maple Grove reps, not the customers located in Maple Grove; CUSTOMER.CITY would answer a different question.
Right - the subquery selects reps 20 and 35 by the rep's own city, and customer 1225 stores REP_NUM 35, so its lines belong on the report.
Nothing is missing - the three matching conditions link all four tables, and the Northfield row is there on purpose.
The subquery's WHERE clause does filter REP; without it the restriction would keep every customer.
questions.takeaway: A restriction filters the table its column comes from - read CITY back as "the rep's city" or "the customer's city" before you trust the result.

sections.title: Aliases, Self-Joins, and Joining Several Tables

blocks.text: Two things make multiple-table queries tiring. The first is typing `CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM` and `INVOICE_LINE.INVOICE_NUM` over and over. The second is harder: sometimes the question you are asked needs the same table twice in one query, and there is no way to tell the two copies apart. An alias solves both problems, and the second one cannot be solved any other way. Learn aliases first and the self-join stops being mysterious.
5-2e Using an alias

You create an alias in the `FROM` clause: write the table name, a space, and the short name you want to use. The word `AS` is optional and most people leave it out. From that point on, you qualify columns with the alias instead of the full table name.

blocks.label: Alias
blocks.text: An alias is a temporary name you give a table inside one statement. It exists only while that statement runs, it is not stored in the database, and it changes nothing about the table itself.

-- GOAL: show the smallest possible use of an alias - a short, temporary name for
-- a table that lives only as long as this one statement.
-- SELECT: C.CUSTOMER_NAME means exactly what CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME means. The
--   alias is already usable here even though it is defined on the next line.
SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: this is where the alias is created - table name, then the short name.
--   The word AS is optional and most people leave it out.
FROM CUSTOMER AS C

-- WHERE: an ordinary condition, written through the alias. One row comes back,
--   Whiskers & Wags Boutique, the only customer of rep 65.
WHERE C.REP_NUM = '65';

That returns one row, Whiskers & Wags Boutique. The `AS` is doing nothing the space would not do on its own, so the rest of this section drops it. Aliases pay off the most when two tables are in play, because every qualified column gets shorter and the matching condition becomes easy to read at a glance.

blocks.starter:
SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NUM, C.CUSTOMER_NAME, R.LAST_NAME, R.RATE
FROM CUSTOMER C, REP ___
WHERE C.REP_NUM = ___.REP_NUM
ORDER BY C.CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.solution:
-- Columns qualified with the SHORT aliases defined below, not the full table names.
SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NUM, C.CUSTOMER_NAME, R.LAST_NAME, R.RATE
-- The aliases are created here: table name, a space, then the short name. Once C
-- and R exist, CUSTOMER and REP are no longer usable names in this statement.
FROM CUSTOMER C, REP R
-- The matching condition, now short enough to read at a glance.
WHERE C.REP_NUM = R.REP_NUM
ORDER BY C.CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.hint: Give REP the alias R in the FROM clause, then use R on both sides of the matching condition.

blocks.text: You get four rows, one per customer, each carrying the last name and rate of the rep who handles the account. Kaiser appears twice because customers 1120 and 1310 are both hers. Hold on to that fact, because it is the whole reason the next lesson exists.

blocks.label: An alias replaces the table name
blocks.text: Once you write `FROM CUSTOMER C`, the name `CUSTOMER` is no longer available in that statement. Writing `CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM` after aliasing produces an error, not a second way to say the same thing.

-- GOAL: a deliberate error. Once a table has an alias, the full table name is no
-- longer available anywhere in that statement.
-- SELECT: WRONG. C is defined below, so CUSTOMER is no longer a usable name and
--   the engine has no table by that name to look the column up in. SQLite says
--   "no such column: CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM"; MySQL and Oracle raise their own
--   version of the same unknown-table error. The fix is to write C.CUSTOMER_NUM.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM

-- FROM: two aliases are defined here, C and R. From this point on they are the
--   only names by which the two tables can be reached.
FROM CUSTOMER C, REP R

-- WHERE: this line is correct - it uses the aliases on both sides. It is only
--   the SELECT list above that breaks the statement.
WHERE C.REP_NUM = R.REP_NUM;
5-2f Joining a table to itself

Here is a real request. The sales manager is routing a rep's travel and wants pairs of customers who share the same rep, so that rep can visit two accounts on one trip. Every piece of information needed sits in CUSTOMER, and yet no single-table `WHERE` clause can answer it.

The reason is that a `WHERE` clause looks at one row at a time. To decide whether Access Pet Center and Companion Care Clinic belong together, the database has to hold two different customer rows side by side and compare them. Getting two rows in play at once means listing the table twice, and listing the table twice means you need aliases to tell the copies apart.

blocks.label: Nothing new is happening
blocks.text: A self-join is not a special command. It is an ordinary join in which both sides happen to be the same table. The aliases are the only thing that makes it possible, which is why 5-2e had to come first.

Listing the table twice also makes every unqualified column name ambiguous. With two copies in play, `CUSTOMER_NUM` on its own could mean either one, and the database refuses to guess. In a self-join you must qualify every column, without exception.

-- GOAL: a second deliberate error, the one that makes aliases compulsory in a
-- self-join rather than merely convenient.
-- SELECT: WRONG. With two copies of CUSTOMER in play, a bare CUSTOMER_NUM could
--   mean the one from copy A or the one from copy B, and the engine refuses to
--   guess. SQLite says "ambiguous column name: CUSTOMER_NUM"; MySQL and Oracle
--   report the same ambiguity in their own wording. Write A.CUSTOMER_NUM.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM

-- FROM: the same table opened twice, under two different names. This is all a
--   self-join is - an ordinary join whose two sides happen to be one table.
FROM CUSTOMER A, CUSTOMER B

-- WHERE: the matching condition between the two copies, correctly qualified.
WHERE A.REP_NUM = B.REP_NUM;

items.title: List the table twice
items.body: Write `FROM CUSTOMER A, CUSTOMER B`. The database now has two independent copies to work with, named A and B.

items.title: Match the copies
items.body: Add `WHERE A.REP_NUM = B.REP_NUM` so a row from A is only considered next to a row from B that shares its rep.

items.title: Restrict the pairs
items.body: Add a second condition on the primary key so each real pair appears exactly once. That step is 5-2g, and the next query shows why it is not optional.

blocks.starter:
SELECT A.CUSTOMER_NUM, B.CUSTOMER_NUM, A.REP_NUM
FROM CUSTOMER A, CUSTOMER B
WHERE A.REP_NUM = B.REP_NUM
ORDER BY A.CUSTOMER_NUM, B.CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.solution:
-- Both copies must be qualified: a bare CUSTOMER_NUM would be ambiguous.
SELECT A.CUSTOMER_NUM, B.CUSTOMER_NUM, A.REP_NUM
-- The same table opened TWICE under two names. That is all a self-join is - an
-- ordinary join whose two sides happen to be one table.
FROM CUSTOMER A, CUSTOMER B
-- Match the copies on the shared rep. With nothing else, this also pairs every
-- row with itself and reports each real pair twice - six rows, not one.
WHERE A.REP_NUM = B.REP_NUM
ORDER BY A.CUSTOMER_NUM, B.CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.hint: Run it as written and count the rows before you read on. Six is more than you wanted.

blocks.text: Six rows come back and only one of them answers the question. Look at what the other five are.

blocks.caption: Every row the unrestricted self-join produces
rows: No, a row paired with itself
Yes, this is the pair you asked for
No, a row paired with itself
No, the same pair in reverse
No, a row paired with itself
No, a row paired with itself

blocks.text: The two problems have different causes. Every customer row matches itself because a rep number is always equal to itself, and every genuine pair shows up twice because the database has no idea which copy you consider first. One extra condition, chosen well, disposes of both.
5-2g Using a self-join on a primary key column

The fix is a second condition, and it goes on the primary key column: `A.CUSTOMER_NUM < B.CUSTOMER_NUM`. Two properties of a primary key are what make this work. It is unique, so no two different rows can tie, and it is never null, so the comparison always has a definite answer. Neither of those is guaranteed for CITY or CUSTOMER_NAME, which is why the restriction belongs on the key.

cards.title: Using <> gives two rows
cards.body: `A.CUSTOMER_NUM <> B.CUSTOMER_NUM` throws out the four self-paired rows, because a row can never differ from itself. It does nothing about ordering, so you still get 1120 with 1310 and 1310 with 1120. Half the result is redundant.

cards.title: Using < gives one row
cards.body: `A.CUSTOMER_NUM < B.CUSTOMER_NUM` is false when the numbers are equal, so self-pairs disappear, and it is true for exactly one of the two orderings, so mirrors disappear too. One condition, both problems solved.

blocks.starter:
SELECT A.CUSTOMER_NUM, A.CUSTOMER_NAME, B.CUSTOMER_NUM, B.CUSTOMER_NAME
FROM CUSTOMER A, CUSTOMER B
WHERE A.REP_NUM = B.REP_NUM
AND A.CUSTOMER_NUM ___ B.CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.solution:
SELECT A.CUSTOMER_NUM, A.CUSTOMER_NAME, B.CUSTOMER_NUM, B.CUSTOMER_NAME
FROM CUSTOMER A, CUSTOMER B
-- The relationship you care about: the two customers share a rep.
WHERE A.REP_NUM = B.REP_NUM
-- The fix, on the PRIMARY KEY. < throws out the self-paired rows (nothing is
-- less than itself) AND picks one direction for each real pair, so each pair is
-- reported exactly once. Six rows collapse to one.
AND A.CUSTOMER_NUM < B.CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.hint: Put a less-than sign between the two primary key columns, then try <> instead and compare the row counts.

blocks.text: One row: 1120 Access Pet Center with 1310 Companion Care Clinic. Swap `<` for `>` and you get one row again, 1310 with 1120, the same pair in the other order. Either direction is correct. What matters is choosing one so each pair is reported once.
The pattern generalizes. Match on the column that describes the relationship you care about, then restrict on the primary key. Here the shared attribute is the category instead of the rep.

blocks.starter:
SELECT A.ITEM_ID, B.ITEM_ID, A.CATEGORY
FROM ITEM A, ITEM B
WHERE A.CATEGORY = B.CATEGORY
AND A.ITEM_ID < B.ITEM_ID;
blocks.solution:
-- The same pattern pointed at a different shared attribute.
SELECT A.ITEM_ID, B.ITEM_ID, A.CATEGORY
FROM ITEM A, ITEM B
-- Match on the column that describes the relationship - here, the category.
WHERE A.CATEGORY = B.CATEGORY
-- Then restrict on the primary key so each pair appears once.
AND A.ITEM_ID < B.ITEM_ID;
blocks.hint: One row comes back, AV07 with FT88, because Habitat is the only category holding two items.

blocks.text: A self-join can also sit alongside other tables. If the sales manager wants the rep name printed next to each pair, bring REP into the same query and link it to either copy of CUSTOMER, since both copies carry the same rep number.

blocks.starter:
SELECT R.LAST_NAME, A.CUSTOMER_NAME, B.CUSTOMER_NAME
FROM CUSTOMER A, CUSTOMER B, REP R
WHERE A.REP_NUM = B.REP_NUM
AND A.REP_NUM = R.REP_NUM
AND A.CUSTOMER_NUM < B.CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.solution:
-- A self-join can sit alongside other tables: three names, two of them the same table.
SELECT R.LAST_NAME, A.CUSTOMER_NAME, B.CUSTOMER_NAME
FROM CUSTOMER A, CUSTOMER B, REP R
-- The two customer copies share a rep.
WHERE A.REP_NUM = B.REP_NUM
-- REP is linked to either copy - both carry the same rep number, so it does not matter which.
AND A.REP_NUM = R.REP_NUM
-- And the primary key condition still keeps each pair to one row.
AND A.CUSTOMER_NUM < B.CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.hint: Three aliases, three conditions: match the copies, attach the rep, restrict the pair.

blocks.text: 5-2h Joining several tables

Now a question that no two tables can answer: which items did each customer order, and how many? Customer names live in CUSTOMER. Item descriptions live in ITEM. Those two tables share no column at all, so there is nothing to match them on. INVOICE and INVOICE_LINE are the bridge between them.
Think of it as a chain. CUSTOMER connects to INVOICE, INVOICE connects to INVOICE_LINE, INVOICE_LINE connects to ITEM. You list all four tables in the `FROM` clause and write one condition per link.

blocks.caption: One condition for each link in the chain
rows: This invoice belongs to that customer
This line appears on that invoice
This line is for that item

items.title: Name every table you need
items.body: Work out which tables hold the columns you want to display and which tables are needed only to reach them. INVOICE and INVOICE_LINE are here mostly as connectors.

items.title: Give each one an alias
items.body: With four tables, unqualified column names get ambiguous fast. Short aliases such as C, I, IL and IT keep the conditions readable.

items.title: Write one condition per link
items.body: A chain of four tables needs three conditions. Count them before you run the query; if you have fewer, a link is missing.

items.title: Add your filters last
items.body: Anything that narrows the result, such as a category or a customer name, goes in the same `WHERE` clause after the linking conditions.

blocks.starter:
SELECT I.INVOICE_NUM, C.CUSTOMER_NAME, IT.DESCRIPTION, IL.NUM_ORDERED
FROM CUSTOMER C, INVOICE I, INVOICE_LINE IL, ITEM IT
WHERE C.CUSTOMER_NUM = I.CUSTOMER_NUM
AND I.INVOICE_NUM = IL.INVOICE_NUM
AND IL.ITEM_ID = ___.ITEM_ID
ORDER BY I.INVOICE_NUM, IT.ITEM_ID;
blocks.solution:
SELECT I.INVOICE_NUM, C.CUSTOMER_NAME, IT.DESCRIPTION, IL.NUM_ORDERED
-- Four tables, all aliased, so the conditions below stay short.
FROM CUSTOMER C, INVOICE I, INVOICE_LINE IL, ITEM IT
-- Link 1 of 3: customer to invoice.
WHERE C.CUSTOMER_NUM = I.CUSTOMER_NUM
-- Link 2: invoice to line item.
AND I.INVOICE_NUM = IL.INVOICE_NUM
-- Link 3: line item to item. Four tables, three links - always one fewer.
AND IL.ITEM_ID = IT.ITEM_ID
ORDER BY I.INVOICE_NUM, IT.ITEM_ID;
blocks.hint: The last link joins INVOICE_LINE to ITEM, so the missing alias is IT.

blocks.text: Six rows, one for every invoice line in the database, each now readable in business terms: Access Pet Center ordered 3 bags of Grain-Free Dry Food and 2 nylon leashes, and so on. Companion Care Clinic does not appear at all, because it has no invoice. That is correct behavior for this kind of join, and 5-5 shows you how to include a customer with nothing to show.

blocks.label: A missing condition does not raise an error
blocks.text: Delete `I.INVOICE_NUM = IL.INVOICE_NUM` from that query and it still runs, returning 18 rows instead of 6. Each of the three invoices gets paired with all six line-and-item combinations. Nothing warns you. Counting your conditions is the defense.
Step 4 said filters go last, so try one. The three linking conditions stay exactly as they were, and a fourth condition narrows the result to a single category of merchandise.

blocks.starter:
SELECT I.INVOICE_NUM, C.CUSTOMER_NAME, IT.DESCRIPTION
FROM CUSTOMER C, INVOICE I, INVOICE_LINE IL, ITEM IT
WHERE C.CUSTOMER_NUM = I.CUSTOMER_NUM
AND I.INVOICE_NUM = IL.INVOICE_NUM
AND IL.ITEM_ID = IT.ITEM_ID
AND IT.CATEGORY = ___
ORDER BY IT.ITEM_ID;
blocks.solution:
SELECT I.INVOICE_NUM, C.CUSTOMER_NAME, IT.DESCRIPTION
FROM CUSTOMER C, INVOICE I, INVOICE_LINE IL, ITEM IT
-- The three links that hold the chain together.
WHERE C.CUSTOMER_NUM = I.CUSTOMER_NUM
AND I.INVOICE_NUM = IL.INVOICE_NUM
AND IL.ITEM_ID = IT.ITEM_ID
-- A fourth condition that is NOT a link: an ordinary filter on the joined rows.
AND IT.CATEGORY = 'Habitat'
ORDER BY IT.ITEM_ID;
blocks.hint: Put the category in single quotes: 'Habitat'. Two rows come back, both on invoice 50712.

blocks.text: Two rows, the Aviary Starter Cage and the Fish Tank Filter Kit, both ordered by Downtown Aquarium & Pets on invoice 50712. Notice the filter did nothing structural. It sits in the same `WHERE` clause as the links and simply drops rows the manager did not ask for.

Chains can be longer. Adding REP in front of CUSTOMER makes five tables and four conditions, and the row count stays at 6 because each customer has exactly one rep. Notice you can also compute a column while you are at it.

blocks.starter:
SELECT R.LAST_NAME, C.CUSTOMER_NAME, IT.DESCRIPTION,
       IL.NUM_ORDERED * IL.QUOTED_PRICE AS EXTENDED
FROM REP R, CUSTOMER C, INVOICE I, INVOICE_LINE IL, ITEM IT
WHERE R.REP_NUM = C.REP_NUM
AND C.CUSTOMER_NUM = I.CUSTOMER_NUM
AND I.INVOICE_NUM = IL.INVOICE_NUM
AND IL.ITEM_ID = IT.ITEM_ID
ORDER BY R.LAST_NAME, IT.DESCRIPTION;
blocks.solution:
SELECT R.LAST_NAME, C.CUSTOMER_NAME, IT.DESCRIPTION,
       -- The calculated line value, named with AS.
       IL.NUM_ORDERED * IL.QUOTED_PRICE AS EXTENDED
-- FIVE tables this time, so four links are needed.
FROM REP R, CUSTOMER C, INVOICE I, INVOICE_LINE IL, ITEM IT
-- Link 1: rep to customer.
WHERE R.REP_NUM = C.REP_NUM
-- Link 2: customer to invoice.
AND C.CUSTOMER_NUM = I.CUSTOMER_NUM
-- Link 3: invoice to line item.
AND I.INVOICE_NUM = IL.INVOICE_NUM

AND IL.ITEM_ID = IT.ITEM_ID

WHERE C.CUSTOMER_NUM = I.CUSTOMER_NUM

questions.scenarioTitle: Access Pet Center on the rep roster
questions.stem: A bookkeeper writes `FROM CUSTOMER C, REP R` and then asks for `CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME` in the SELECT list. What happens when the statement runs?
options: It runs normally, because the full table name and the alias both remain available
It fails, because the alias replaces the table name for the whole statement
It runs but lists every customer twice, once under each form of the name
It fails, because aliases are permitted only when a table appears twice
optionNotes: An alias is a replacement rather than an addition; the original table name goes out of scope in that query.
Correct: after `CUSTOMER C` is written, the engine reports no such column: CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME.
How a column is named never duplicates rows; the row count comes from the join conditions.
Aliases are legal in any query, including single-table ones; they are only required for a self-join.
questions.takeaway: An alias renames a table for the length of the statement, so qualify every column with the alias once you define one.

questions.scenarioTitle: Valerie Kaiser's two Maple Grove accounts
questions.stem: `FROM CUSTOMER A, CUSTOMER B WHERE A.REP_NUM = B.REP_NUM` returns six rows against the KimTay data. Why are five of them unwanted?
options: Because customers 1225 and 1420 carry balances the query should have filtered out first
Because REP was left out, so rep numbers were matched against the wrong column
Because four rows pair a customer with itself and one row repeats a pair in reverse
Because the matching condition should have compared the rep numbers with an inequality
optionNotes: Balances play no part here; every customer row qualifies because a rep number always equals itself.
REP is not needed at all, since both sides of this join are copies of CUSTOMER.
Correct: 1120, 1225, 1310 and 1420 each pair with themselves, and 1310 with 1120 mirrors 1120 with 1310.
An inequality on REP_NUM would return customers handled by different reps, which is the opposite question.
questions.takeaway: An unrestricted self-join returns self-pairs and both orderings of every real pair, so it always needs a second condition.

questions.scenarioTitle: Companion Care Clinic paired twice
questions.stem: A student replaces the pair restriction with `A.CUSTOMER_NUM <> B.CUSTOMER_NUM` and runs the self-join again. What comes back?
options: One row, because `<>` and `<` remove exactly the same rows from the result
Zero rows, because no two KimTay customer numbers differ from one another
Six rows, because `<>` has no effect on a self-join over a primary key
Two rows, 1120 with 1310 and 1310 with 1120, the same pair listed both ways
optionNotes: `<>` removes only the self-paired rows and keeps both orderings of every genuine pair, so it returns one row more than `<` does.
Customer numbers are unique, so `<>` is true for every combination of two different rows.
`<>` does have an effect: it removes the four self-paired rows, bringing the result from six rows down to two.
Correct: only `<` keeps a single ordering per pair, which is what gets the answer down to one row.
questions.takeaway: Use `<` rather than `<>` on the primary key so each pair of rows is reported exactly once.

questions.scenarioTitle: Downtown Aquarium & Pets invoice detail
questions.stem: In the chain over CUSTOMER, INVOICE, INVOICE_LINE and ITEM, the condition `I.INVOICE_NUM = IL.INVOICE_NUM` is deleted by accident. What does the warehouse manager see?
options: Eighteen rows and no error, because every invoice is now matched to every invoice line
An error message reporting that a join condition is missing from the WHERE clause
The correct six rows, because the primary keys still connect those tables automatically
Zero rows, because INVOICE and INVOICE_LINE can no longer be connected to each other
optionNotes: Correct: three invoices times the six matched line-and-item rows produces eighteen rows.
SQL never requires a join condition, so a missing one is a logic error rather than a syntax error.
Key columns connect tables only when you write the matching condition yourself in the WHERE clause.
Tables left unmatched multiply rows instead of cancelling them, so you get more rows, never fewer.
questions.takeaway: Count your linking conditions before running a multi-table query; a missing one inflates the result silently.
