blocks.text: Every query you have written so far builds one result table from one `SELECT`. A set operation works differently. You write two complete `SELECT` statements, and a keyword between them tells SQL how to fold the two result tables into one. The reason to reach for one is that some business questions are really questions about two lists rather than one condition: which customers are on this list or that one, which are on both, which are on the first but missing from the second.

blocks.caption: The four set operations
rows: In the first list, the second, or both
In the first list, the second, or both
In the first list but not the second

blocks.label: Union compatibility
blocks.text: Two `SELECT` statements can be combined only if they are union compatible: each one returns the same number of columns, in the same order, and the columns that line up hold compatible kinds of data. The column names do not have to match. The combined result takes its headings from the first `SELECT`.

That rule exists because the answer has to be a single table with a single set of headings. If the first `SELECT` returns two columns and the second returns one, there is no sensible way to line them up, and every SQL engine rejects the statement before running anything. Column types are a different story, and here the engines genuinely disagree. SQLite, the engine in the sandboxes below, enforces the column count but is relaxed about types, so it will cheerfully stack a `BALANCE` value underneath a `CUSTOMER_NAME` and hand the whole thing back as one column. MySQL is just as permissive and converts both sides to a common type. Oracle is the strict one: it rejects the mismatch with `ORA-01790: expression must have same datatype as corresponding expression`. Line your columns up on purpose rather than trusting the engine to catch you.
UNION: everything on either list

KimTay's office manager wants one mailing list that covers every customer served by rep 20 together with every customer that has an invoice on file. Some customers qualify on both counts, and each of those should still appear once. That is exactly what `UNION` does.

-- GOAL: one combined list - every customer served by rep 20, together with every
-- customer that has an invoice, each appearing only once.
-- SELECT: the first of two complete SELECT statements. Its two columns fix the
--   shape of the answer, and its headings are the headings of the whole result.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: the first statement reads CUSTOMER.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: first set - the customers of rep 20. That is 1120 and 1310.
WHERE REP_NUM = '20'

-- UNION: folds the two results into one and removes duplicate rows. Both sides
--   must be union compatible: same number of columns, same order, compatible
--   types. The names do not have to match.
UNION

-- SELECT: the second complete statement begins here. Two columns again.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: it happens to read the same table, but it does not have to.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: second set - the customers that appear in INVOICE. That is 1120, 1225
--   and 1420. Customer 1120 is on both lists, and UNION keeps one copy of it,
--   so the combined answer is four rows rather than five.
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM IN (SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM FROM INVOICE)

-- ORDER BY: a set operation is ONE statement, so it gets ONE ORDER BY, and it
--   belongs after the last SELECT. Sorting the first half on its own is an error.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

The first `SELECT` returns 1120 and 1310. The second returns 1120, 1225 and 1420. Access Pet Center (1120) is on both lists, and `UNION` keeps one copy of it, so the combined answer is four rows rather than five.

blocks.caption: Result of the UNION above

blocks.label: One ORDER BY, at the very end
blocks.text: A set operation is a single statement, so it gets a single `ORDER BY`, and that `ORDER BY` belongs after the last `SELECT`. Sorting the first `SELECT` on its own is an error. SQLite answers `ORDER BY clause should come after UNION not before`.
UNION ALL: keep the duplicates
`UNION ALL` stacks the two results and stops there. Nothing is compared and nothing is thrown away. Ask for every city that appears in `CUSTOMER` or in `REP` and the difference shows up immediately.

-- GOAL: every city named in either table, with nothing removed.
-- SELECT / FROM: the first list - the four city values stored in CUSTOMER.
SELECT CITY FROM CUSTOMER

-- UNION ALL: stacks the two lists and stops there. Nothing is compared and
--   nothing is discarded, so a city held by several rows is listed several times.
UNION ALL

-- SELECT / FROM: the second list - the three city values stored in REP. Seven
--   rows come back in all: Maple Grove, Northfield, Maple Grove, Brookville,
--   then Maple Grove, Maple Grove, Brookville.
SELECT CITY FROM REP;

That returns seven rows: Maple Grove, Northfield, Maple Grove, Brookville from `CUSTOMER`, then Maple Grove, Maple Grove, Brookville from `REP`. Change the one keyword and the answer shrinks to the three distinct cities.

-- GOAL: the same two lists, with the one keyword changed, to see what duplicate
-- removal costs and buys.
-- SELECT / FROM: the first list - the cities in CUSTOMER.
SELECT CITY FROM CUSTOMER

-- UNION: same stacking as UNION ALL, plus a duplicate check. Seven rows shrink
--   to the three distinct cities. That check is real work, which is the reason
--   UNION ALL exists at all.
UNION

-- SELECT / FROM: the second list - the cities in REP.
SELECT CITY FROM REP

-- ORDER BY: sorts the combined three-row result. It sits at the very end of the
--   whole statement, never inside either half.
ORDER BY CITY;

blocks.caption: Result of the UNION: three rows

cards.title: Use UNION
cards.body: When the same real-world thing could be described by both queries and you want it counted once. Mailing lists, combined rosters, any "who qualifies under either rule" question.

cards.title: Use UNION ALL
cards.body: When you know the two lists cannot overlap, or when the repeats are the point and you are about to count them. It skips the duplicate-removal work, so it is also the faster of the two.

blocks.text: INTERSECT: only the overlap
Swap in `INTERSECT` and the same two lists answer a different question: which customers are served by rep 20 and also have an invoice on file?

-- GOAL: the overlap - customers who are served by rep 20 AND have an invoice.
-- SELECT: the first statement, two columns.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: it reads CUSTOMER.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: first set - rep 20's customers, 1120 and 1310.
WHERE REP_NUM = '20'

-- INTERSECT: keeps only rows produced by BOTH sides, and removes duplicates.
--   Order does not matter here: swapping the two halves asks the same question.
INTERSECT

-- SELECT: the second statement, the same two columns in the same order.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: it reads CUSTOMER too.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: second set - the invoiced customers, 1120, 1225 and 1420. Only 1120 is
--   on both lists, so one row comes back. 1310 belongs to rep 20 but has never
--   been billed, and 1225 and 1420 have invoices but belong to other reps.
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM IN (SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM FROM INVOICE);

One row comes back: 1120, Access Pet Center. Companion Care Clinic (1310) is served by rep 20 but has never been invoiced, so it drops out. Downtown Aquarium & Pets and Whiskers & Wags have invoices but belong to other reps, so they drop out too.
EXCEPT: on the first list, missing from the second
`EXCEPT` subtracts. It returns the rows produced by the first `SELECT` that the second `SELECT` did not also produce. That is how the bookkeeper finds rep 20's customers who have never been billed.

-- GOAL: the subtraction - rep 20's customers who have never been billed.
-- SELECT: the first statement, two columns.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: it reads CUSTOMER.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: first set - rep 20's customers, 1120 and 1310.
WHERE REP_NUM = '20'

-- EXCEPT: keeps the rows the first statement produced that the second did not
--   also produce. Order matters here in a way it never does for UNION or
--   INTERSECT: reverse the halves and you are asking which invoiced customers do
--   not belong to rep 20, which answers 1225 and 1420 instead. Oracle spells
--   this operation MINUS.
EXCEPT

-- SELECT: the second statement, matching shape.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: it reads CUSTOMER as well.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: second set - the invoiced customers. Removing them from the first set
--   leaves one row, 1310 Companion Care Clinic.
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM IN (SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM FROM INVOICE);

The answer is one row: 1310, Companion Care Clinic. Order matters here in a way it never does for `UNION` or `INTERSECT`. Put the two `SELECT` statements the other way round and you are asking a different question, "which invoiced customers do not belong to rep 20", and you get 1225 and 1420 instead.

blocks.label: Oracle spells it MINUS
blocks.text: Oracle's traditional keyword for this operation is `MINUS` rather than `EXCEPT`, with the same meaning and the same sensitivity to order. Oracle 21c added `EXCEPT` as well, but `MINUS` is what you will meet in most Oracle code and in most Oracle-based textbooks. MySQL added `EXCEPT` and `INTERSECT` in 8.0.31. SQLite understands `EXCEPT` and rejects `MINUS` with `near "SELECT": syntax error`, so write `EXCEPT` in the sandbox.
When the two SELECT statements do not line up
This is the mistake you are most likely to make, so learn to recognise the error message rather than guessing at it:

-- GOAL: a deliberate error - the mistake you are most likely to make with a set
-- operation, so that you recognise the message instead of guessing at it.
-- SELECT: the first statement returns TWO columns.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: it reads CUSTOMER.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- UNION: the two halves are not union compatible, and the engine rejects the
--   statement here without executing anything. SQLite says "SELECTs to the left
--   and right of UNION do not have the same number of result columns".
UNION

-- SELECT: the second statement returns ONE column, and that is the whole problem.
--   The fix is always the same - add or remove a column until the counts agree.
SELECT REP_NUM

-- FROM: it reads REP.
FROM REP;

Two columns above the line, one below it. SQLite refuses before executing anything and says `SELECTs to the left and right of UNION do not have the same number of result columns`. MySQL and Oracle say the same thing in their own words. The fix is always the same: add or remove a column so the two counts agree.
The two SELECT statements can read different tables

Nothing requires both halves to come from the same table. As long as the shapes match, you can stack results from anywhere. Here is a single Brookville contact list drawn from both `CUSTOMER` and `REP`.

-- GOAL: a single Brookville contact list, drawn from two different tables. The
-- halves of a union do not have to read the same table - only to match in shape.
-- SELECT: two columns, each renamed with AS. Headings always come from the FIRST
--   SELECT, which is why it is worth putting the aliases here.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM AS ID_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME AS NAME

-- FROM: the first half reads CUSTOMER.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: restricts the first half to Brookville - customer 1420.
WHERE CITY = 'Brookville'

-- UNION: stacks the two lists and drops duplicates. Two columns on each side,
--   and a number lines up with a number, text with text, so the two are
--   union compatible.
UNION

-- SELECT: the second half returns a rep number and a last name. It never mentions
--   ID_NUM or NAME, and does not need to - only the count, order and types matter.
SELECT REP_NUM, LAST_NAME

-- FROM: the second half reads REP.
FROM REP

-- WHERE: restricts the second half to Brookville - rep 65, Perez.
WHERE CITY = 'Brookville'

-- ORDER BY: sorts the combined result, and must use the heading the first SELECT
--   established. ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM would be an error here.
ORDER BY ID_NUM;

Two rows come back, 1420 Whiskers & Wags Boutique and 65 Perez, under the headings `ID_NUM` and `NAME`. Notice that the second `SELECT` never mentions those names. Headings always come from the first `SELECT`, which is why it is worth putting your `AS` aliases there. The 1420 row sorts ahead of the 65 row because both id columns hold characters, not numbers, and '1' comes before '6'.

-- The first of two complete SELECT statements. Its columns fix the shape.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME
FROM CUSTOMER
-- First set: rep 20's customers.
WHERE REP_NUM = '20'
-- INTERSECT keeps only rows produced by BOTH sides. Order does not matter here.
INTERSECT
-- The second statement: same number of columns, same order, same types.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME
FROM CUSTOMER
-- Second set: the customers that have an invoice. Only the overlap survives.
WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM IN (SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM FROM INVOICE);

-- First set: the Ohio students.
SELECT STUDENT_ID, LAST_NAME
FROM STUDENT
WHERE HOME_STATE = 'OH'
-- UNION combines and drops duplicates, so a student who qualifies on both counts
-- is still listed once.

FROM STUDENT
-- Second set: the students leasing at property P200.

blocks.text: A subquery in a `WHERE` clause usually returns a list of values, and until now you have tested membership in that list with `IN`. `ALL` and `ANY` let you do something different: compare one value against every value in the list at once, using `>`, `<`, `>=` or `<=` instead of membership. `BALANCE > ALL (...)` means larger than every value the subquery produced. `BALANCE > ANY (...)` means larger than at least one of them.

blocks.label: These do not run in the sandbox
blocks.text: SQLite does not implement `ALL` or `ANY` as subquery comparisons, and the two fail in slightly different places. `> ALL (SELECT ...)` stops at `near "ALL": syntax error`, because `ALL` is a SQLite keyword in the wrong position. `> ANY (SELECT ...)` and `> SOME (SELECT ...)` stop one word later at `near "SELECT": syntax error`, because `ANY` and `SOME` are not SQLite keywords at all and the parser reads them as a column name. Either way nothing executes. MySQL and Oracle support all three. Every `ALL` or `ANY` statement in this lesson is shown in a plain code block for that reason, and each one is followed by a rewrite that does run, so you can see the answer for yourself.
ALL: bigger than every one of them

KimTay's credit manager wants the customers whose balance is larger than the balance of every single customer rep 20 handles. Rep 20's customers are Access Pet Center at 3512.50 and Companion Care Clinic at 0.00. In MySQL or Oracle you would write this:

-- GOAL: the customers whose balance beats the balance of EVERY customer rep 20
-- handles. Written the MySQL or Oracle way; this is a syntax error in SQLite.
-- SELECT: three columns, including the balance being tested, so you can check the
--   comparison by eye.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE

-- FROM: one table - the subquery reads the same table again, separately.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: the subquery returns rep 20's balances, 3512.50 and 0.00. "Greater than
--   ALL" means the row's balance must beat every value in that list, which is
--   the same as beating the largest one. Read it out loud as "balance greater
--   than all of these".
WHERE BALANCE > ALL (SELECT BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20');

Read it out loud as "balance greater than all of these". A row survives only if its balance beats 3512.50 and also beats 0.00. Beating the largest of the two is therefore the whole test, and that is the key to rewriting it.

blocks.label: The rewrite that always works
blocks.text: `> ALL (subquery)` asks the value to beat the largest thing in the list, so it is the same as `> (SELECT MAX(...))`. `> ANY (subquery)` asks the value to beat the smallest thing in the list, so it is the same as `> (SELECT MIN(...))`. Those rewrites run everywhere, including SQLite.

-- GOAL: the same question, rewritten so it runs everywhere, SQLite included.
-- SELECT: the same three columns.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE

-- FROM: the outer query reads CUSTOMER.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: because "greater than ALL" only ever tests the top of the list, MAX
--   collapses the subquery to the single number 3512.50, and an ordinary
--   comparison does the rest. One row clears it - 1420, at 4820.75.
WHERE BALANCE > (SELECT MAX(BALANCE) FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20')

-- ORDER BY: sorts whatever survives by customer number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

blocks.caption: One row beats every balance rep 20 handles

blocks.text: ANY: bigger than at least one of them
Change the one keyword and the bar drops a long way. Now a row needs to beat only the weakest value in the list.

-- GOAL: change one keyword and the bar drops a long way - now a balance need only
-- beat the WEAKEST value in the list. MySQL or Oracle; a syntax error in SQLite.
-- SELECT: the same three columns as the ALL version.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE

-- FROM: the outer query reads CUSTOMER.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: the subquery returns the same two balances, 3512.50 and 0.00. "Greater
--   than ANY" means greater than at least one of them, which is the same as
--   greater than the smallest. SOME is an exact synonym for ANY.
WHERE BALANCE > ANY (SELECT BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20');

The smallest balance among rep 20's customers is Companion Care Clinic's 0.00, so the test collapses to "balance greater than 0.00". Three customers clear it. Companion Care Clinic itself does not, because 0.00 is not greater than 0.00.

-- GOAL: the ANY version rewritten to run everywhere.
-- SELECT: the same three columns.
SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE

-- FROM: the outer query reads CUSTOMER.
FROM CUSTOMER

-- WHERE: "greater than ANY" only ever tests the bottom of the list, so MIN
--   collapses the subquery to 0.00 and the test becomes "balance greater than
--   0.00". Three customers clear it. Companion Care Clinic does not, because
--   0.00 is not greater than 0.00.
WHERE BALANCE > (SELECT MIN(BALANCE) FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20')

-- ORDER BY: sorts the three surviving rows by customer number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER_NUM;

blocks.caption: Three rows beat at least one balance rep 20 handles

blocks.label: SOME means ANY
blocks.text: The SQL standard defines `SOME` as an exact synonym for `ANY`, and MySQL and Oracle accept both. `> SOME (...)` and `> ANY (...)` behave identically. Textbooks sometimes prefer `SOME` because "greater than any" reads in English as though it should mean "greater than all of them", which is the single most common misreading of this operator.
Every combination, and what to write instead
There are only six shapes to learn, and each one has a rewrite that runs in the sandbox. Work out which end of the list the comparison is really testing, and the rewrite follows.

blocks.caption: Translating ALL and ANY

blocks.text: The last two rows are worth pausing on. `= ANY` is the operator `IN` you have been using since 5-2a, written a longer way, and `<> ALL` is `NOT IN`. When you meet them in someone else's code, translate them on sight.

blocks.label: One place the rewrite differs
blocks.text: If the subquery returns no rows at all, `> ALL` is true for every row, because there is nothing to fail against, while `> ANY` is false for every row. An aggregate over zero rows returns NULL, so both rewrites make the comparison unknown and return nothing. That means the `MIN` rewrite still agrees with `> ANY`, since both hand back an empty result, but the `MAX` rewrite disagrees with `> ALL`, which would have handed back every row. The seed data always gives these subqueries something to chew on, so it will not bite you here, but know which of the two rewrites is the inexact one.

blocks.text: This lesson names three things. The first you have already been doing since Module 3 without a formal name for it. The second fixes a gap the first one leaves. The third is what SQL hands you when you forget to say how two tables connect, and knowing it on sight will save you an afternoon one day.
5-5a Inner join: the one you already know

When you match rows in two tables on a shared value and keep only the pairs that match, you are performing an inner join. SQL has explicit words for it, `INNER JOIN` and `ON`, and they say out loud what the older comma-and-`WHERE` style leaves implied.

-- GOAL: the very first join of this module, rewritten in the modern INNER JOIN
-- ... ON form. Same four rows, different words.
-- SELECT: the three output columns, qualified as always.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, REP.LAST_NAME

-- FROM: the two tables and the matching condition now sit on one line. INNER JOIN
--   names the second table and ON carries the condition, so the WHERE clause is
--   left free for real business filters. Forgetting ON is a syntax error you
--   cannot miss, which is why this form is worth preferring.
FROM CUSTOMER INNER JOIN REP ON CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM

-- ORDER BY: sorts the four rows by customer number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM;

blocks.caption: Four customers, each with the rep that serves it

blocks.text: The `ON` clause holds the matching condition. The `WHERE` clause is now free for actual filtering, which is the main practical reason to prefer this form: with three or four tables in a query, keeping the plumbing in `ON` and the business rules in `WHERE` is the difference between a query you can read and one you cannot. The word `INNER` is optional, so `FROM CUSTOMER JOIN REP ON ...` means the same thing.
Inner joins chain. To put a description on every invoice line you walk from `INVOICE` through `INVOICE_LINE` to `ITEM`, one `JOIN ... ON` per hop.

-- GOAL: put a description on every invoice line by walking INVOICE to
-- INVOICE_LINE to ITEM. Inner joins chain - one JOIN ... ON per hop.
-- SELECT: one column from each of the three tables.
SELECT INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM, ITEM.DESCRIPTION, INVOICE_LINE.NUM_ORDERED

-- FROM: link 1 - each invoice is joined to its own line items. Everything to the
--   left of the next INNER JOIN behaves as a single combined table.
FROM INVOICE INNER JOIN INVOICE_LINE ON INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM = INVOICE_LINE.INVOICE_NUM

-- Link 2 - that combined result is then joined to ITEM. Three tables need two
-- JOIN ... ON clauses, the same count as the two matching conditions the older
-- comma-and-WHERE form would have needed. Six rows come back.
INNER JOIN ITEM ON INVOICE_LINE.ITEM_ID = ITEM.ITEM_ID

-- ORDER BY: by invoice, then by description within each invoice.
ORDER BY INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM, ITEM.DESCRIPTION;
Six rows come back, one per invoice line, from Grain-Free Dry Food on 50710 through Fish Tank Filter Kit on 50712.

blocks.label: Inner join
blocks.text: A join that returns only the rows that have a match on both sides. A row with no partner in the other table is dropped from the result, silently, with no warning of any kind. That silence is the whole reason the next lesson exists.
5-5b Outer join: keep the rows that did not match
Watch what the silence costs. Ask an inner join for every customer and its invoices.

-- GOAL: ask an inner join for every customer and its invoices, and watch what
-- silently goes missing.
-- SELECT: two customer columns and the invoice number.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM

-- FROM: INNER JOIN keeps only the pairs that match on both sides. Customer 1310
--   has no row in INVOICE, so it has no partner and is dropped - with no warning
--   of any kind. Four customers go in, three rows come out.
FROM CUSTOMER INNER JOIN INVOICE ON CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM = INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM

-- ORDER BY: sorts the three surviving rows by customer number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM;

blocks.caption: Three rows. KimTay has four customers.

blocks.text: Companion Care Clinic (1310) is gone. It is a real customer with a 10000.00 credit limit, but it has never been invoiced, so it has no partner row in `INVOICE` and the inner join discards it. If the office manager reads that result as "our customer list", the one account with nothing billed against it is invisible. An outer join is the fix.

-- GOAL: the same question, with the unmatched customer kept in the answer.
-- SELECT: the same three columns as the inner join above.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM

-- FROM: LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the table written on the LEFT of the
--   keyword, matched or not. CUSTOMER is on the left, so CUSTOMER is the table
--   being protected. Where a customer has no invoice, SQL invents one row's
--   worth of NULLs for the columns that came from the right-hand table, so 1310
--   comes back with a null invoice number. Four rows this time.
FROM CUSTOMER LEFT JOIN INVOICE ON CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM = INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM

-- ORDER BY: sorts all four rows by customer number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM;

blocks.caption: Four rows. The unmatched customer comes back with a NULL.

blocks.text: `LEFT JOIN` keeps every row from the table on the left of the keyword, matched or not. Where there was no match, SQL invents one row's worth of NULLs for the columns that came from the right-hand table. This is the first time in this course you will see a NULL in a result, and it is worth being clear about where it came from: nothing in KimTay's data is missing, and every column of every shipped row holds a real value. The NULL is manufactured by the join to fill a hole.

cards.title: LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN
cards.body: `A LEFT JOIN B` keeps everything in A. `A RIGHT JOIN B` keeps everything in B. They are mirror images, so `FROM INVOICE RIGHT JOIN CUSTOMER ON ...` returns the exact same four rows as the `LEFT JOIN` above. Most people write `LEFT JOIN` and put the table they care about first.

cards.title: FULL OUTER JOIN
cards.body: Keeps unmatched rows from both sides at once. SQLite supports it from version 3.39 and so does Oracle. MySQL does not have it at all: there you emulate it with a `LEFT JOIN` and a `RIGHT JOIN` combined by `UNION`, which is the set operation from 5-3 earning its keep.

blocks.text: Against the shipped data a `FULL OUTER JOIN` of `CUSTOMER` and `INVOICE` returns the same four rows as the `LEFT JOIN`, because every invoice does point at a real customer, so there is nothing unmatched on the right. The sandbox below adds an orphan invoice on purpose so you can see the difference the third join makes.
There is one more move to learn, and it is the reason outer joins pay for themselves. Keep the unmatched rows, then filter down to only those, and you have a query that finds gaps.

-- GOAL: find the gaps - the rows that have no match at all - in two steps.
-- SELECT: only the customer columns. The invoice column is used for testing and
--   would be null on every row that survives anyway.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME

-- FROM: step 1 - LEFT JOIN keeps all four customers, filling the INVOICE columns
--   with NULL wherever no invoice matched.
FROM CUSTOMER LEFT JOIN INVOICE ON CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM = INVOICE.CUSTOMER_NUM

-- WHERE: step 2 - keep only the rows the join had to fill in. IS NULL is the only
--   way to test for a null; = NULL never matches anything, not even another null.
--   Here the test can be true only for a customer the join failed to match, so
--   the whole query reads as "customers with no invoice". One row: 1310.
WHERE INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM IS NULL;

One row: Companion Care Clinic. `IS NULL` is the only way to test for a NULL, because `= NULL` never matches anything, not even another NULL. Here the test can only be true for a row the join failed to match, so the whole query reads as "customers with no invoice". Point the same pattern at StayWell and it finds rooms nobody has leased, or leases nobody has paid on.

blocks.label: An outer join does not always add NULLs
blocks.text: `ITEM LEFT JOIN INVOICE_LINE` returns six rows with no NULL anywhere, because every one of KimTay's five items has been ordered at least once, and CF21 has been ordered on two invoices so it appears twice. An outer join promises to keep unmatched rows. It does not promise there are any, and it will happily return more rows than the left table has.
5-5c The product: what you get with no join condition
List two tables and give SQL no instruction about how they relate, and it does the only thing it can: it pairs every row on the left with every row on the right.

-- GOAL: see the product - what SQL does when you never say how two tables relate.
-- SELECT: one identifying column from each table, so the pattern is easy to read.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, REP.REP_NUM

-- FROM: two tables listed with a comma and nothing else. There is no WHERE clause
--   anywhere, so nothing restricts the pairings and every customer is paired with
--   every rep: 4 x 3 = 12 rows, eight of them nonsense. This is the accident you
--   cause by adding a table to FROM and forgetting its matching condition.
FROM CUSTOMER, REP

-- ORDER BY: sorting by both columns makes the regular repeating pattern - the
--   symptom of an accidental product - obvious on sight.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, REP.REP_NUM;

KimTay has four customers and three reps, so the result is 4 times 3, which is twelve rows: 1120 with 20, 1120 with 35, 1120 with 65, then 1225 with all three, and so on. Every customer appears matched to every rep, including the reps who do not serve it, so eight of the twelve rows are nonsense.

blocks.label: Product (Cartesian product, cross join)
blocks.text: The product of two tables is every possible pairing of a row from the first with a row from the second. If one table has m rows and the other has n, the product has m times n rows. `FROM A, B` with no matching condition produces it, and so does the explicit `FROM A CROSS JOIN B`, which returns the same twelve rows and has the advantage of looking deliberate.

You will almost never want a product on purpose. You will produce one by accident, usually by adding a table to the `FROM` list and forgetting to add its matching condition. The symptom is unmistakable once you know it: the row count explodes and the same value repeats down a column in a regular pattern. If a query over four customers hands you twelve rows, count your join conditions before you debug anything else.
Supply the missing condition and the product collapses back into an inner join. This is the older syntax, and it is exactly the first query in this lesson wearing different clothes.

-- GOAL: supply the missing condition and watch the product collapse back into an
-- inner join. This is the first query of the lesson wearing different clothes.
-- SELECT: two customer columns and the rep's last name.
SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, REP.LAST_NAME

-- FROM: the same comma-separated pair of tables that produced the 12-row product.
FROM CUSTOMER, REP

-- WHERE: this single line is the entire difference. It throws away the eight
--   pairings where the customer's rep number does not equal the rep's, leaving
--   the same four rows the INNER JOIN ... ON version returned.
WHERE CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM

-- ORDER BY: sorts the four rows by customer number.
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM;

Four rows, identical to the `INNER JOIN ... ON` version. Both forms are legal everywhere and you will meet both in real code. Prefer `INNER JOIN ... ON`, because forgetting the `ON` clause is a syntax error you cannot miss, whereas forgetting a line of the `WHERE` clause is a silent product.

items.title: Ask what must appear in the answer
items.body: If every customer has to be listed whether or not it has been billed, you need an outer join. If only billed customers belong in the answer, an inner join is correct and the missing rows are not a bug.

items.title: Put the table you must keep on the left
items.body: Then write `LEFT JOIN`. Reaching for `RIGHT JOIN` usually means you listed the tables in the wrong order.

items.title: Write one ON clause per join
items.body: Two tables need one condition, three tables need two, four tables need three. Count them before you run anything.

items.title: Check the row count against what you expected
items.body: More rows than the left table has means the right table matched several times, which may be correct. A row count equal to m times n means you lost a join condition.

VALUES ('50713', '9999', '2026-06-16');

-- CUSTOMER has 4 rows, REP has 3.

-- Then run the rows themselves, and finally add the missing condition
--      WHERE CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM
-- to collapse the product into the inner join you actually wanted.

SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NAME, REP.LAST_NAME
-- The older comma-and-WHERE form. Listing two tables with no condition would
-- produce the twelve-row product...
FROM CUSTOMER, REP
-- ...and this single line is the whole difference between that and a real join.
WHERE CUSTOMER.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM
ORDER BY CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.hint: The product is twelve rows, 4 times 3. Adding the `WHERE` condition cuts it to the four rows that are true, one per customer. `FROM CUSTOMER CROSS JOIN REP` also returns twelve and states the intent openly.

blocks.starter:
-- Two gap-finding questions for StayWell. Use LEFT JOIN for both.
-- a) Every room, with its lease id, including rooms nobody leases.
-- b) Every lease, with its payments, including leases with no payment.
-- Part (a) is started for you: ROOM's key is two columns, so the ON
-- clause needs both, joined with AND.

SELECT ROOM.PROPERTY_ID, ROOM.ROOM_NUM, LEASE.LEASE_ID
FROM ROOM LEFT JOIN LEASE ON
blocks.solution:
SELECT ROOM.PROPERTY_ID, ROOM.ROOM_NUM, LEASE.LEASE_ID
-- ROOM is on the left, so every room is kept whether or not it has been leased.
FROM ROOM LEFT JOIN LEASE
  -- The ON condition needs BOTH key columns, because a room is identified by the
  -- property and the room number together. One of them alone would over-match.
  ON ROOM.PROPERTY_ID = LEASE.PROPERTY_ID AND ROOM.ROOM_NUM = LEASE.ROOM_NUM
ORDER BY ROOM.PROPERTY_ID, ROOM.ROOM_NUM;
blocks.hint: Part (a) gives five rows and P200 room 101 has an empty `LEASE_ID`, so it is the vacant one. Part (b) also gives five rows, but for the opposite reason: L001 appears twice because it has two payments, and L004 appears once with an empty payment.

I can add `WHERE <right column> IS NULL` to turn an outer join into a gap-finding query, and I know `= NULL` would never work
I know MySQL has no `FULL OUTER JOIN` and can be given a `LEFT JOIN UNION RIGHT JOIN` instead

questions.scenarioTitle: KimTay builds one mailing list
questions.stem: KimTay's office manager needs a single mailing list. The first `SELECT` returns the two customers served by rep 20, which are 1120 and 1310. The second `SELECT` returns the three customers that have an invoice, which are 1120, 1225 and 1420. She combines them with `UNION`. How many rows come back, and why?
options: Five rows, because the two result tables are stacked exactly as written
Two rows, because `UNION` keeps only the customers that appear on both lists
Four rows, because 1120 appears on both lists and `UNION` keeps one copy of it
Three rows, because the second `SELECT` overwrites the first one's results
optionNotes: That is the `UNION ALL` count. Plain `UNION` removes duplicate rows before returning the result.
That describes `INTERSECT`, which would return 1120 alone. `UNION` keeps rows from either list.
Correct. 1120, 1225, 1310 and 1420 each appear once, because `UNION` collapses the duplicate 1120.
Neither `SELECT` overwrites the other. A set operation combines both results into one table.
questions.takeaway: `UNION` returns everything on either list with duplicate rows removed, so overlapping rows appear once.

questions.scenarioTitle: Counting items across two KimTay invoices
questions.stem: The warehouse manager lists the `ITEM_ID` values on invoice 50710 (CF21 and DG04) and on invoice 50711 (CF21 and GR15), combining them with `UNION ALL`. She then reruns the identical statement with `UNION`. What does she see?
options: Four rows with `UNION ALL` and three rows with `UNION`, because CF21 is on both invoices
Four rows both times, because both keywords stack the two results unchanged
Three rows both times, because SQL never returns the same item identifier twice
Two rows with `UNION ALL`, because it returns only the items the invoices share
optionNotes: Correct. `UNION ALL` keeps the repeated CF21; `UNION` removes it and leaves CF21, DG04 and GR15.
`UNION ALL` stacks unchanged, but plain `UNION` removes the duplicate row, so the counts differ.
Duplicate removal is what `UNION` does and what `UNION ALL` deliberately skips, so the counts differ.
That is the behaviour of `INTERSECT`. `UNION ALL` keeps everything from both queries.
questions.takeaway: `UNION ALL` is the raw stack of both results; `UNION` is that stack with duplicate rows removed.

questions.scenarioTitle: Companion Care Clinic has never been billed
questions.stem: A KimTay bookkeeper wants rep 20's customers that have no invoice on file. She puts the rep 20 query first and the has-an-invoice query second, joined by `EXCEPT`, and gets Companion Care Clinic. A colleague swaps the two `SELECT` statements and reruns it. What happens?
options: The same single row comes back, because `EXCEPT` compares two lists regardless of order
An error, because `EXCEPT` requires the larger result table to be written first
No rows at all, because reversing the operands always empties an `EXCEPT` result
A different answer, 1225 and 1420, because the query now asks which invoiced customers are not rep 20's
optionNotes: `UNION` and `INTERSECT` ignore order, but `EXCEPT` subtracts the second list from the first.
Neither operand has to be larger. The statement runs; it answers a different question.
Reversal changes the question but does not empty it. Two invoiced customers belong to other reps.
Correct. `EXCEPT` subtracts, so putting the invoiced list first asks the opposite question.
questions.takeaway: `EXCEPT` is directional: the first `SELECT` supplies the candidates and the second removes from them.

questions.scenarioTitle: Rewriting a credit report for the sandbox
questions.stem: A KimTay analyst has an Oracle report containing `WHERE BALANCE > ALL (SELECT BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20')` and needs it to run in the course sandbox, where the statement is a syntax error. Rep 20's customers hold balances of 3512.50 and 0.00. Which rewrite returns the same rows?
options: Replace it with `WHERE BALANCE IN (SELECT BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20')`
Replace it with `WHERE BALANCE > (SELECT MAX(BALANCE) FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20')`
Replace it with `WHERE BALANCE > (SELECT MIN(BALANCE) FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20')`
Replace it with `WHERE BALANCE > (SELECT AVG(BALANCE) FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20')`
optionNotes: `IN` tests for an exact match on a value in the list, not for being larger than the whole list.
Correct. Beating every value in the list is the same as beating the largest one, so `MAX` is the rewrite.
`MIN` is the rewrite for `> ANY`. It would return three customers instead of the one that `ALL` returns.
The average is neither the largest nor the smallest value, so it answers a question nobody asked.
questions.takeaway: `> ALL (subquery)` means "beats the largest value in the list", which rewrites to `> (SELECT MAX(...))`.

questions.scenarioTitle: Reading ANY out loud at StayWell
questions.stem: A StayWell manager writes `WHERE MONTHLY_RENT > ANY (SELECT MONTHLY_RENT FROM ROOM WHERE PROPERTY_ID = 'P100')` in MySQL. Property P100 has rooms renting at 595.00 and 450.00. She expects only rooms above 595.00. What does the query actually return?
options: Only the rooms renting above 595.00, matching her expectation exactly
Nothing at all, because `ANY` requires the subquery to return a single value
Four rooms, every room renting above 450.00, because `ANY` needs to beat only the smallest value
The two P100 rooms themselves, because `ANY` restricts the result to the subquery's own rows
optionNotes: That is what `> ALL` would return, and it is only two rooms. `> ANY` sets the bar at the smallest value, not the largest.
`ANY` is built for multi-row subqueries; a single-value subquery needs no `ANY` at all.
Correct. Beating at least one value means beating 450.00, so P100 101, P200 101, P200 201 and P200 202 qualify.
The subquery only supplies comparison values; it does not limit which rows the outer query may return.
questions.takeaway: `> ANY` sets a low bar: a row qualifies by beating the smallest value in the list, not the largest.

questions.scenarioTitle: Inherited code at KimTay
questions.stem: A developer inherits a query containing `WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM <> ALL (SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM FROM INVOICE)` and must port it to the SQLite sandbox, which rejects `ALL`. What does that condition mean, and what replaces it?
options: It means the customer number differs from at least one invoice's, replaced by `<> ANY`
It means the customer number matches every invoice's, replaced by an equality comparison
It means the customer number is missing from the invoice list, replaced by `NOT IN (subquery)`
It means the customer has more than one invoice, replaced by a `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` clause
optionNotes: `<> ANY` is a much weaker test that almost any row passes; it is not equivalent and does not fix the engine problem.
`<> ALL` asserts the value differs from every entry, which is the opposite of matching them all.
Correct. Differing from every value in the list is the definition of `NOT IN`, and it returns customer 1310.
Nothing here counts anything. `<> ALL` is a value comparison against a list, not an aggregate test.
questions.takeaway: `= ANY` is `IN` written the long way and `<> ALL` is `NOT IN`; translate them on sight.

questions.scenarioTitle: The customer report that lost a customer
questions.stem: KimTay's office manager runs an inner join of `CUSTOMER` and `INVOICE` on `CUSTOMER_NUM` and gets three rows, although the company has four customers. Companion Care Clinic (1310) is missing. What explains it?
options: Customer 1310 has a zero balance, and joins discard rows whose numeric columns are zero
Customer 1310 has no matching row in `INVOICE`, and an inner join keeps only matched pairs
The join condition names the wrong column, so one of the four customers failed to match
`INVOICE` holds only three rows, so any join with it can never return more than three
optionNotes: A zero balance is an ordinary value. Joins match on the `ON` condition and ignore every other column.
Correct. 1310 has never been invoiced, so the inner join drops it silently; `LEFT JOIN` brings it back.
`CUSTOMER_NUM` is the correct shared column. The row is missing because no invoice references it.
Row counts on either side do not cap a join. A left outer join of the same two tables returns four rows.
questions.takeaway: An inner join silently drops any row with no partner, so a short result is a signal to check for unmatched rows.

questions.scenarioTitle: StayWell hunts for a vacant room
questions.stem: StayWell wants every room listed together with its lease, including rooms nobody has leased. The manager writes `FROM ROOM LEFT JOIN LEASE ON ROOM.PROPERTY_ID = LEASE.PROPERTY_ID AND ROOM.ROOM_NUM = LEASE.ROOM_NUM`. There are five rooms and four leases. What comes back?
options: Four rows, because only rooms with a matching lease can appear in a join result
Five rows, with P200 room 101 showing an empty `LEASE_ID` because nobody leases it
Twenty rows, because listing two tables always pairs every row with every other row
Five rows, with the empty lease id replaced automatically by the string 'none'
optionNotes: That is the inner join count. `LEFT JOIN` keeps every row of the left table whether or not it matched.
Correct. All five rooms survive, and the one room with no lease gets NULLs in the `LEASE` columns.
A product needs no join condition. This query supplies one, so it matches instead of pairing everything.
SQL fills unmatched columns with NULL, never with a substitute word. If you want a label there, you have to put it there yourself.
questions.takeaway: `LEFT JOIN` keeps every row from the left table and fills the right-hand columns with NULLs when nothing matched.

questions.scenarioTitle: Twelve rows from four customers
questions.stem: A KimTay developer writes `SELECT CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM, REP.REP_NUM FROM CUSTOMER, REP;` and gets twelve rows, with each of the four customer numbers appearing three times. What has happened?
options: The `CUSTOMER` table has hidden duplicate rows that need to be cleaned up before joining
A left outer join ran by default and manufactured eight extra rows to fill the gaps
`REP` was queried three times, once per rep, and the results were stacked with `UNION ALL`
No join condition was given, so SQL produced the product: 4 customers times 3 reps
optionNotes: `CUSTOMER` holds four distinct rows. The repetition is created by the query, not present in the table.
No join type is applied by default, and an outer join never invents pairings that the data does not support.
Nothing here stacks results. All twelve rows come from a single `SELECT` over two tables.
Correct. With nothing in `ON` or `WHERE` to connect them, every customer is paired with every rep.
questions.takeaway: Two tables in `FROM` with no matching condition produce the product, m times n rows, and it is nearly always a bug.

questions.scenarioTitle: Finding KimTay's never-billed customers
questions.stem: The bookkeeper needs a list of customers that have never been invoiced, and she wants it as a single query over `CUSTOMER` and `INVOICE`. Which approach returns exactly Companion Care Clinic?
options: Inner join the two tables, then add `WHERE INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM IS NULL` to the result
Left join `CUSTOMER` to `INVOICE`, then add `WHERE INVOICE.INVOICE_NUM IS NULL`
Cross join the two tables, then add `WHERE CUSTOMER.BALANCE = 0` to isolate the row
Right join `CUSTOMER` to `INVOICE`, then add `WHERE CUSTOMER.CUSTOMER_NUM IS NULL`
optionNotes: An inner join has already discarded the unmatched rows, so the `IS NULL` test can never be true and returns nothing.
Correct. The outer join keeps the unmatched customer, and `IS NULL` narrows the result to exactly those rows.
A cross join pairs all twelve combinations, and filtering on balance answers a question about money, not billing.
`FROM CUSTOMER RIGHT JOIN INVOICE` keeps every invoice, and testing the customer side finds orphan invoices instead.
questions.takeaway: Outer join first to keep the unmatched rows, then test the other table's column with `IS NULL` to keep only the gaps.

matchers.heading: Sort the result into the operation that produced it
matchers.prompt: Each card describes what came back from a query over two or three tables. Decide whether that result was produced by an inner join, a left outer join, or a product with no join condition.

cards.text: Five rows from `ROOM` and `LEASE`, where P200 room 101 shows no lease id while the other four rooms show theirs.
