blocks.text: Module 5 rested on one idea: the answer you need is almost never sitting in a single table. KimTay keeps the customer in `CUSTOMER`, the sale in `INVOICE`, the line items in `INVOICE_LINE`, and the product in `ITEM`, so a question as ordinary as "what did Access Pet Center buy?" has to travel across four tables. You now have several ways to make that trip, and a good part of the skill is knowing which one a question calls for.

cards.title: Reaching sideways
cards.body: A join, `IN`, `EXISTS`, or a nested subquery all answer questions of the form "rows from here, filtered or described by data over there." A join widens a row, because the result can carry columns from both tables; `IN` and `EXISTS` do not, because the second table only decides which rows qualify.

cards.title: Stacking results
cards.body: `UNION`, `INTERSECT`, and `EXCEPT` answer questions of the form "these rows together, or only the shared ones, or only the ones missing from the other list." They lengthen a result rather than widening it, and both sides have to be union compatible.

blocks.text: Here is the whole module in one list. If a line reads as unfamiliar, the lesson it came from is worth a second pass before you go on.

items: Join two tables by matching a foreign key to a primary key, either in the `WHERE` clause or with `INNER JOIN ... ON`.
Qualify a column as `table.column` whenever that name exists in both tables, or the DBMS rejects the query as ambiguous.
Give a table an alias in the `FROM` clause, then use that alias everywhere else in the query.
Use `IN` or `EXISTS` when the second table only decides which rows qualify and contributes no columns to the output.
Nest a subquery inside another subquery when the answer takes two hops, and read it from the inside out.
Join a table to itself, using two aliases, when you need to compare one row of a table with another row of the same table.
Stack two union-compatible results with `UNION`, keep only the shared rows with `INTERSECT`, or subtract one from the other with `EXCEPT`.
Compare one value against a whole column of values with `ALL` and `ANY` on MySQL or Oracle, and rewrite both with `MAX` or `MIN` on SQLite.
Keep unmatched rows with an outer join, and expect `NULL` in every column that came from the side with no match.
Spot an accidental product: when the linking condition is missing, rows multiply instead of matching.
Predict how many rows a multi-table query should return before you run it, then check.

blocks.label: Engine note
blocks.text: The sandbox on this page runs SQLite, and SQLite does not accept `> ALL (subquery)` or `> ANY (subquery)` at all: it stops with a syntax error at the keyword. MySQL and Oracle do accept them. The runnable equivalents return exactly the same rows: `> ALL (SELECT BALANCE ...)` is `> (SELECT MAX(BALANCE) ...)`, and `> ANY (SELECT BALANCE ...)` is `> (SELECT MIN(BALANCE) ...)`. Write whichever form your engine accepts, and know why the two agree.

One last query pulls several of these together. It has to keep a customer that has no invoice, which rules out an inner join, and it has to count something that can be missing, which rules out `COUNT(*)`. Try it before you reveal the answer.

blocks.starter:
-- List every KimTay customer with the number of invoices they have,
-- including the customer who has never been invoiced.
-- Four rows come back, and one of the counts is 0.
blocks.solution:
-- COUNT(I.INVOICE_NUM) counts VALUES, so an unmatched customer scores 0.
-- COUNT(*) would count the null-padded row and wrongly report 1.
SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NAME, COUNT(I.INVOICE_NUM) AS INVOICE_COUNT
FROM CUSTOMER C
-- LEFT JOIN keeps the customers with no invoices in the answer at all.
LEFT JOIN INVOICE I ON C.CUSTOMER_NUM = I.CUSTOMER_NUM
-- Group by the key as well as the name, so two customers sharing a name stay apart.
GROUP BY C.CUSTOMER_NUM, C.CUSTOMER_NAME
ORDER BY C.CUSTOMER_NAME;
blocks.hint: Companion Care Clinic has no invoice, so an inner join drops it and a `LEFT JOIN` keeps it. Count `I.INVOICE_NUM` rather than `*`: the padded row is still a row, so `COUNT(*)` would report 1 for the clinic instead of 0.

blocks.text: Everything that follows in this course assumes you can reach across tables without thinking twice about it. Reading a multi-table statement and saying out loud how many rows it returns, and why, is the single best way to keep that skill sharp.

These are the words this module added to your vocabulary. Only one of them names something you were already writing before this module: the nested subquery from lesson 4-4. The rest are new here, and several of them name distinctions that get lost if you only ever say "joining tables."

blocks.caption: Terms for reaching across tables
rows: A query that combines rows from two or more tables by matching values in a column the tables share.
A join that keeps only rows with a match on both sides; `FROM A, B WHERE A.k = B.k` and `A INNER JOIN B ON A.k = B.k` are two spellings of the same thing.
A join that also keeps unmatched rows, from the left table, the right table, or both, filling the missing columns with `NULL`.
A join of a table to itself, written with two different aliases so one table can play two roles in a single query.
A short alternate name you give a table in the `FROM` clause and then use everywhere else in the query.
Every row of one table paired with every row of another, which is what you get when the linking condition is missing: 3 reps and 4 customers produce 12 rows.

blocks.caption: Terms for subqueries and set operations
rows: All rows appearing in either of two union-compatible results, with duplicates kept only once.
Only the rows that appear in both of two union-compatible results.
The rows of the first result that do not appear in the second; `EXCEPT` in SQLite and SQL Server, `MINUS` in Oracle.
Two results are union compatible when they have the same number of columns and matching columns hold the same kind of data; the column names need not match.
An operator that is true when its subquery returns at least one row, used when another table decides which rows qualify but supplies no columns.
A subquery that refers to a column of the outer query, so the DBMS has to evaluate it once for every row the outer query considers.

Compares a value against every value a subquery returns; `> ALL` is true only when the value beats the largest of them. MySQL and Oracle only: SQLite rejects `> ALL (subquery)` with a syntax error, so in the sandbox below write `> (SELECT MAX(...) ...)` instead.

Compares a value against the values a subquery returns and is true if at least one comparison holds; `> ANY` is true when the value beats the smallest of them. MySQL and Oracle only, exactly like `ALL`: the sandbox equivalent is `> (SELECT MIN(...) ...)`.

blocks.label: Union compatible is about shape, not names
blocks.text: `SELECT CITY FROM REP` and `SELECT CITY FROM CUSTOMER` are union compatible because each returns one column of city text. `SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER` and `SELECT PROPERTY_NAME FROM PROPERTY` would be union compatible too, even though the columns carry different names, because both return one column of names. What breaks compatibility is a different number of columns, or columns that do not line up in kind: `SELECT CITY FROM REP UNION SELECT CITY, STATE FROM CUSTOMER` fails with "SELECTs to the left and right of UNION do not have the same number of result columns."

Three of these terms are easier to recognize running than defined. The sandbox starts with the self-join; use Show solution to add the union and the correlated subquery underneath it, then run all three at once.

blocks.starter:
-- Alias plus self-join: two KimTay customers that share a city.
SELECT F.CUSTOMER_NAME AS FIRST_ONE, S.CUSTOMER_NAME AS SECOND_ONE, F.CITY
FROM CUSTOMER F, CUSTOMER S
WHERE F.CITY = S.CITY
  AND F.CUSTOMER_NUM < S.CUSTOMER_NUM;
blocks.solution:
-- Alias plus self-join: two KimTay customers that share a city.
-- Both copies are aliased and both output columns are renamed for readability.
SELECT F.CUSTOMER_NAME AS FIRST_ONE, S.CUSTOMER_NAME AS SECOND_ONE, F.CITY
-- One table, opened twice under two names.
FROM CUSTOMER F, CUSTOMER S
-- The shared attribute that defines the pair.
WHERE F.CITY = S.CITY
  -- The primary key condition that removes self-pairs and reversed duplicates.
  AND F.CUSTOMER_NUM < S.CUSTOMER_NUM;

-- Union compatible: one column of city text on each side.
SELECT CITY FROM REP
-- UNION removes duplicates, so a city both tables use appears once.
UNION
SELECT CITY FROM CUSTOMER
-- One ORDER BY for the whole statement, at the end.
ORDER BY CITY;

-- Correlated subquery: the inner query names C.CUSTOMER_NUM from the outer row.
SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NAME
FROM CUSTOMER C
-- SELECT 1 rather than SELECT * - EXISTS never uses the value, so anything does.
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM INVOICE I WHERE I.CUSTOMER_NUM = C.CUSTOMER_NUM);
blocks.hint: The self-join returns one row, Access Pet Center paired with Companion Care Clinic in Maple Grove. The union returns three cities. The correlated `EXISTS` returns the three customers that have an invoice, leaving out Companion Care Clinic.

blocks.text: Notice what the aliases buy you in that first statement. `CUSTOMER F` and `CUSTOMER S` are the same table twice, and without two names there would be no way to say "this customer's city equals that customer's city." Notice also that once a table has an alias, the alias replaces the table name: after `FROM CUSTOMER F`, writing `CUSTOMER.CITY` is an error, and SQLite reports it as `no such column: CUSTOMER.CITY`.

Ten questions covering the whole module. They are harder than the checks inside the lessons: several of them hand you a finished statement and ask what it returns against the real KimTay and StayWell data, which is exactly what an exam question looks like.

blocks.label: How to read a statement you did not write
blocks.text: Read the `FROM` clause first and count the tables. Then look for a condition that links them. If there is no linking condition you are looking at a product, and the row count is one table's rows times the other's. If there is one, ask which rows have no match, because that is where inner and outer joins part company.
The scratch pad below is loaded with both databases. Use it after you commit to an answer, not before: predicting a result and being wrong teaches you more than watching the engine do it first.

blocks.starter:
-- Scratch pad. Predict the answer, then check it here.
-- Start with the row counts you should be able to state from memory:
SELECT 'REP' AS TABLE_NAME, COUNT(*) AS ROW_COUNT FROM REP
UNION ALL SELECT 'CUSTOMER', COUNT(*) FROM CUSTOMER
UNION ALL SELECT 'INVOICE', COUNT(*) FROM INVOICE
UNION ALL SELECT 'INVOICE_LINE', COUNT(*) FROM INVOICE_LINE
UNION ALL SELECT 'ITEM', COUNT(*) FROM ITEM;
blocks.solution:
-- A row-count audit built entirely out of UNION ALL. Each SELECT invents a label
-- column and counts one table; UNION ALL stacks them without checking duplicates,
-- which is what you want when every row is deliberately different.
SELECT 'REP' AS TABLE_NAME, COUNT(*) AS ROW_COUNT FROM REP
-- Only the FIRST SELECT needs the AS aliases - the headings come from it.
UNION ALL SELECT 'CUSTOMER', COUNT(*) FROM CUSTOMER
UNION ALL SELECT 'INVOICE', COUNT(*) FROM INVOICE
UNION ALL SELECT 'INVOICE_LINE', COUNT(*) FROM INVOICE_LINE
UNION ALL SELECT 'ITEM', COUNT(*) FROM ITEM;

-- The same audit for the StayWell database.
SELECT 'MANAGER' AS TABLE_NAME, COUNT(*) AS ROW_COUNT FROM MANAGER
UNION ALL SELECT 'PROPERTY', COUNT(*) FROM PROPERTY
UNION ALL SELECT 'ROOM', COUNT(*) FROM ROOM
UNION ALL SELECT 'STUDENT', COUNT(*) FROM STUDENT
UNION ALL SELECT 'LEASE', COUNT(*) FROM LEASE
UNION ALL SELECT 'PAYMENT', COUNT(*) FROM PAYMENT;
blocks.hint: KimTay: 3 reps, 4 customers, 3 invoices, 6 invoice lines, 5 items. StayWell: 2 managers, 2 properties, 5 rooms, 4 students, 4 leases, 4 payments. Those eleven numbers let you predict most row counts in your head.

blocks.text: Work through the questions below. Each explanation names the specific misconception behind every wrong option, so read all four notes even when you answered correctly.

Five exercises over KimTay and StayWell. Work each one out first, and write down the number of rows you expect before you run anything. The count is part of the answer: a query that returns 12 rows when you predicted 3 is telling you a linking condition went missing.
1. The invoice list the office actually wants

KimTay's billing clerk wants one line per invoice showing the invoice number, the invoice date, the customer's name, and the last name of the rep who handles that customer. Three tables have to appear in the `FROM` clause, and the customer sits between the other two. How many rows should come back?
2. What one rep's accounts are buying

List the description of every item that appears on an invoice belonging to a customer of rep 20. Four tables this time. Before you run it, work out which of rep 20's two customers can contribute anything at all, and how many invoices that leaves you with; that number tells you whether `DISTINCT` can change the answer on this data. Write it with `DISTINCT` anyway, because the query has to stay correct the day rep 20 picks up a second invoice that repeats an item.
3. Every student, paid or not

StayWell wants each student's last name, first name, and the total of their payments so far, and every student has to appear even if they have paid nothing yet. Every student does have a lease, so the requirement bites on the payment side, and exactly one student qualifies. What does the total column hold for that student, and why is it not `0`?
4. The room nobody has rented

List every StayWell room that has never appeared on a lease, and write it twice. The `NOT EXISTS` version can report the property, room number and room type, because it selects from `ROOM` and only tests `LEASE`. The `EXCEPT` version cannot: `LEASE` has no `ROOM_TYPE` column, so the two sides are union compatible only on `PROPERTY_ID` and `ROOM_NUM`, and putting a third column on the left makes the statement fail outright. Both versions find the same room, one with three columns and one with two.
5. Where KimTay sells but does not staff

List every city that has a KimTay customer but no KimTay rep. This is a difference between two single-column results, so check first that the two `SELECT` statements are union compatible. Exactly one city qualifies, and it is worth asking who covers that account.

items: You wrote down an expected row count for each exercise before running it.
Every column name that exists in two of the tables you referenced is qualified with a table name or an alias.
Each pair of joined tables has a condition linking them, so a four-table query carries three linking conditions.
Exercise 3 uses an outer join to `PAYMENT`, because an inner one would silently drop the student you were told to keep.
You can say in one sentence why exercise 4's two versions find the same room, and why only one of them can show that room's type.

blocks.text: Both databases are loaded in the sandbox below. The starter holds the five prompts as comments; Show solution replaces them with worked answers, including both versions of exercise 4.

blocks.starter:
-- Both databases are loaded. Write each answer under its comment,
-- run it, then compare the row count with the one you predicted.

-- 1. Every invoice with its date, customer name and rep last name.


-- 2. The distinct items on invoices belonging to rep 20's customers.


-- 3. Every student and the total paid so far, including one who has paid nothing.


-- 4. Rooms that have never appeared on a lease.


-- 5. Cities where KimTay has a customer but no rep.
blocks.solution:
-- 1. Three rows, one per invoice.
SELECT I.INVOICE_NUM, I.INVOICE_DATE, C.CUSTOMER_NAME, R.LAST_NAME
-- Three tables, so two links.
FROM INVOICE I, CUSTOMER C, REP R
-- Link 1: invoice to the customer it belongs to.
WHERE I.CUSTOMER_NUM = C.CUSTOMER_NUM
  -- Link 2: that customer to the rep who serves it.
  AND C.REP_NUM = R.REP_NUM
ORDER BY I.INVOICE_NUM;

-- 2. Two rows: the dry food and the leash. Rep 20's only invoiced customer
-- is Access Pet Center, and it has a single invoice, so DISTINCT has nothing
-- to collapse today; it is here to keep the query right tomorrow.
SELECT DISTINCT T.DESCRIPTION
-- Four tables to travel from a rep number all the way to an item description.
FROM ITEM T, INVOICE_LINE L, INVOICE I, CUSTOMER C
-- The three links, walked backwards: item to line, line to invoice, invoice to customer.
WHERE T.ITEM_ID = L.ITEM_ID
  AND L.INVOICE_NUM = I.INVOICE_NUM
  AND I.CUSTOMER_NUM = C.CUSTOMER_NUM
  -- The restriction, on a column that never appears in the output.
  AND C.REP_NUM = '20'
ORDER BY T.DESCRIPTION;

-- 3. Four rows. Jason Park's total is null, not zero: SUM over no rows
-- has nothing to add up. COALESCE(SUM(P.AMOUNT), 0) would print 0 instead.
SELECT S.LAST_NAME, S.FIRST_NAME, SUM(P.AMOUNT) AS PAID
FROM STUDENT S
-- Two LEFT JOINs chained: a student with no lease survives the first, and then
-- survives the second as well, because a null carries straight through.
LEFT JOIN LEASE L ON S.STUDENT_ID = L.STUDENT_ID
LEFT JOIN PAYMENT P ON L.LEASE_ID = P.LEASE_ID
-- Group by the key as well as the names, so two students sharing a name stay apart.
GROUP BY S.STUDENT_ID, S.LAST_NAME, S.FIRST_NAME
ORDER BY S.LAST_NAME;

-- 4. One row: P200 room 101, Single.
SELECT R.PROPERTY_ID, R.ROOM_NUM, R.ROOM_TYPE
FROM ROOM R
-- NOT EXISTS: keep the room only when the inner search comes back empty. The
-- inner query is correlated - it names R from the outer row.
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM LEASE L
                  -- Both key columns are needed to identify one room.
                  WHERE L.PROPERTY_ID = R.PROPERTY_ID
                    AND L.ROOM_NUM = R.ROOM_NUM);

-- 4 again, written as a difference. Same room, but only the two columns
-- ROOM and LEASE have in common: adding ROOM_TYPE to the left side would
-- break union compatibility and the statement would not run at all.
SELECT PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM FROM ROOM
-- EXCEPT keeps rows from the first result that the second did not also produce.
EXCEPT
SELECT PROPERTY_ID, ROOM_NUM FROM LEASE;

-- 5. One row: Northfield.
SELECT CITY FROM CUSTOMER
-- Order matters for EXCEPT: swapping the halves asks a different question.
EXCEPT
SELECT CITY FROM REP;
blocks.hint: Expected counts: 3 rows, 2 rows, 4 rows, 1 row, 1 row. Rep 20 has one invoiced customer and therefore one invoice, so exercise 2 returns two descriptions with or without `DISTINCT`; more than two means the rep 20 filter is missing or a linking condition is. In exercise 3 every student already has a lease, so the join that can drop Jason Park is the one to `PAYMENT`: if you get three rows, make that join `LEFT`.

blocks.text: If you want one more pass, redo exercise 1 in explicit `INNER JOIN ... ON` form and confirm you get the same three rows. Being fluent in both spellings matters, because the code you inherit will use whichever one its author preferred.

quizzes.heading: Module 5 cumulative review: joins, subqueries, and set operations

questions.scenarioTitle: The rep list that came back too long
questions.stem: KimTay's billing clerk wants each rep next to the customers that rep handles, and writes `SELECT R.LAST_NAME, C.CUSTOMER_NAME FROM REP R, CUSTOMER C;` with no other clause. There are 3 reps and 4 customers on file. What comes back?
options: Twelve rows, because every rep is paired with every customer when no linking condition is given
Four rows, one per customer, because the DBMS matches REP_NUM by itself when both tables have it
Three rows, one per rep, because REP is named first in the FROM clause and drives the result
No rows at all, because a query over two tables is rejected without an explicit INNER JOIN clause
optionNotes: With nothing linking the tables the DBMS forms the product, 3 times 4, and the clerk has to hunt for the 4 real pairs inside 12 rows.
No engine guesses a join for you; matching REP_NUM values is something you have to state in a WHERE or ON clause.
Table order in the FROM clause changes nothing about the row count; this is not a loop with an outer table.
The comma form is legal SQL and runs happily, which is exactly the danger: a missing condition is a silent bug, not an error.
questions.takeaway: A multi-table FROM clause with no linking condition is not an error, it is a product, and the rows multiply instead of matching.

questions.scenarioTitle: Companion Care Clinic's invoice count
questions.stem: Companion Care Clinic (1310) has no invoice. A clerk runs `SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NAME, COUNT(*) FROM CUSTOMER C LEFT JOIN INVOICE I ON C.CUSTOMER_NUM = I.CUSTOMER_NUM GROUP BY C.CUSTOMER_NUM, C.CUSTOMER_NAME;` and checks the clinic's row. What number does it show?
options: Zero, because COUNT(*) skips any row that an outer join had to pad with nulls
The clinic does not appear at all, because there is no invoice row to count for it
One, because COUNT(*) counts the padded row itself even though every invoice column in it is null
An error, because COUNT(*) cannot be used in a query that contains a LEFT JOIN
optionNotes: COUNT(*) counts rows, not values, so it has no way to notice that the invoice half of the row is empty.
Keeping that row is the whole point of the LEFT JOIN; the clinic is present, and only the count misleads.
The outer join produced one row for the clinic, so COUNT(*) reports 1, while COUNT(I.INVOICE_NUM) reports the honest 0.
The combination is perfectly legal, which is why this mistake survives long enough to reach a report.
questions.takeaway: After an outer join, count a column from the optional side rather than COUNT(*), or every unmatched row reports one instead of none.

questions.scenarioTitle: The unsold item at KimTay's warehouse
questions.stem: The warehouse manager hunts for dead stock with `SELECT DESCRIPTION FROM ITEM I WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM INVOICE_LINE L WHERE L.ITEM_ID = I.ITEM_ID);` and the grid comes back empty. What does that empty result mean?
options: All five items qualify, because NOT EXISTS reverses the test and therefore matches every row
No rows at all, because every one of the five items appears on at least one invoice line
One row, the aviary starter cage, because it was ordered on only a single invoice
An error, because the subquery selects the literal 1 instead of naming a real column
optionNotes: NOT EXISTS is false for an item that does appear on a line, and all five do, so nothing survives the filter.
AV07, CF21, DG04, FT88 and GR15 all appear in INVOICE_LINE, so there is no dead stock and zero rows is the right answer.
Being ordered once still counts as being ordered; NOT EXISTS asks whether any matching line exists, not how many.
SELECT 1 is idiomatic inside EXISTS, because EXISTS only asks whether a row came back, never what was in it.
questions.takeaway: An empty result is an answer, not a failure: NOT EXISTS returning nothing means every row on the outer side had a match.

questions.scenarioTitle: Downtown Aquarium and the mailing list
questions.stem: A mailing list needs every city KimTay touches. A clerk compares `SELECT CITY FROM REP UNION SELECT CITY FROM CUSTOMER;` with the same statement written `UNION ALL`. REP holds Maple Grove, Maple Grove, Brookville; CUSTOMER holds Maple Grove, Northfield, Maple Grove, Brookville. What do the two return?
options: Both return seven rows, because UNION removes duplicates only inside one SELECT, not across both
Both return three rows, because SQL always removes duplicate rows from any query result
UNION returns seven rows and UNION ALL returns three, since ALL narrows the list to the shared cities
UNION returns three rows and UNION ALL returns seven, because UNION removes duplicates and ALL keeps them
optionNotes: UNION deduplicates the combined result, so the four Maple Grove values collapse into one across both sides.
A plain SELECT keeps duplicates; only UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT and DISTINCT remove them.
ALL is the opposite of narrowing: it means keep everything, repeats included. Narrowing to shared rows is INTERSECT.
Three distinct cities remain, Brookville, Maple Grove and Northfield, while UNION ALL stacks 3 plus 4 rows untouched.
questions.takeaway: UNION removes duplicates and pays for the sort that finds them; UNION ALL keeps every row, so use it when duplicates cannot occur or do not matter.

questions.scenarioTitle: The join that lost Companion Care Clinic
questions.stem: Asked for every customer alongside any invoice they have, including customers with none, a developer writes `SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NAME, I.INVOICE_NUM FROM INVOICE I LEFT JOIN CUSTOMER C ON I.CUSTOMER_NUM = C.CUSTOMER_NUM;`. What actually comes back?
options: Four rows, because a LEFT JOIN preserves every row of both tables regardless of the order written
Three rows, one per invoice, and Companion Care Clinic is missing because LEFT keeps the rows of INVOICE
Three rows plus one all-null row, because the unmatched customer still occupies a place in the result
An error, because the optional table in a LEFT JOIN has to be written to the left of the keyword
optionNotes: LEFT preserves one side only, the table named before the keyword, which here is INVOICE rather than CUSTOMER.
Every invoice has a customer, so nothing gets padded, and the customer with no invoice never enters the result at all.
The clinic contributes no row whatsoever, so there is no null row to notice; the mistake is invisible in the output.
The statement is valid SQL and runs; it simply answers a different question than the one that was asked.
questions.takeaway: In a LEFT JOIN the preserved table is the one written first, so keeping the rows you care about depends on the order you list the tables.

questions.scenarioTitle: Access Pet Center against rep 20's other account
questions.stem: Rep 20's two accounts have balances 3512.50 and 0.00. On MySQL a manager runs `SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE BALANCE > ALL (SELECT BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20');`. What comes back, and how would you ask the same question in this page's SQLite sandbox?
options: Access Pet Center and Whiskers and Wags Boutique, since ALL is satisfied by beating any one balance
Every customer with a balance above zero, because 0.00 is the value that ALL ends up comparing against
Whiskers and Wags Boutique alone, and greater than (SELECT MAX(BALANCE) ...) is the runnable equivalent
Nothing at all, because ALL requires its subquery to return exactly one value and this one returns two
optionNotes: Beating one value is ANY. Access Pet Center's 3512.50 does not beat its own balance, so ALL rules it out.
That describes greater than ANY, which effectively uses the smallest value; ALL uses the largest, here 3512.50.

Only 4820.75 is greater than both balances, and beating every value is the same test as beating the maximum. SQLite will not parse the ALL form at all, so the MAX rewrite is the only version that runs on this page.
ALL exists precisely for multi-row subqueries; a subquery returning one value would have no need of it.
questions.takeaway: Greater than ALL means greater than the maximum and greater than ANY means greater than the minimum, which is also how you rewrite both for SQLite.

questions.scenarioTitle: The two Maple Grove accounts, listed twice
questions.stem: A self-join finds KimTay customers that share a city: `SELECT A.CUSTOMER_NAME, B.CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER A, CUSTOMER B WHERE A.CITY = B.CITY AND A.CUSTOMER_NUM <> B.CUSTOMER_NUM;`. Access Pet Center (1120) and Companion Care Clinic (1310) are both in Maple Grove, and no other city holds two customers. What comes back, and what would changing `<>` to `<` do?
options: Two rows, the same pair with the roles swapped, and the strict less-than keeps only one row per pair
One row, and less-than would return nothing, because no customer number is smaller than itself
Four rows, because each customer is also paired with itself before the condition is applied
Two rows, and less-than changes nothing, since it only affects the order the result is sorted in
optionNotes: 1120 with 1310 and 1310 with 1120 both satisfy the inequality, and requiring A.CUSTOMER_NUM < B.CUSTOMER_NUM keeps just the first.
One row is what less-than produces; the inequality shown produces two, and less-than certainly does not produce none.
The condition A.CUSTOMER_NUM <> B.CUSTOMER_NUM is what removes the self-pairings, and it removes them before you see them.
Less-than is a filter, not a sort, and it cuts the mirrored duplicate out of the result entirely.
questions.takeaway: A self-join on equality produces each pair twice plus the self-pairings, so a strict inequality between the keys keeps exactly one row per pair.

questions.scenarioTitle: The query KimTay's DBMS refused
questions.stem: Trying to match reps with customers, someone writes `SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, LAST_NAME FROM REP, CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = REP_NUM;` and presses Run. What happens?
options: It runs and returns four matched rows, since both columns are named REP_NUM and clearly refer to each other
It runs and returns twelve rows, because a column compared with itself is true for every pair
It runs but returns no rows, because the two REP_NUM columns are declared in different tables
It is rejected as an ambiguous column name, because REP_NUM exists in both tables and neither use is qualified
optionNotes: The DBMS cannot tell which REP_NUM you mean on either side of the equals sign, so it refuses instead of guessing.
That would be the outcome if the reference were unambiguous, such as REP.REP_NUM = REP.REP_NUM, but the query never gets that far.
Both columns are CHAR(2) holding the same kind of value; the problem is the name, not the data.
Qualifying both sides as REP.REP_NUM = CUSTOMER.REP_NUM fixes it and turns the product into the four-row join that was intended.
questions.takeaway: When a column name exists in more than one table in the FROM clause, every use of it must be qualified, and the DBMS refuses rather than choosing for you.

questions.scenarioTitle: The Sycamore Court room nobody has leased
questions.stem: StayWell runs `SELECT R.PROPERTY_ID, R.ROOM_NUM FROM ROOM R WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM LEASE L WHERE L.PROPERTY_ID = R.PROPERTY_ID AND L.ROOM_NUM = R.ROOM_NUM);` over 5 rooms and 4 leases. What comes back, and what makes that subquery correlated?
options: Nothing, because four leases against five rooms means the subquery always finds a match somewhere
All five rooms, because the subquery is evaluated once, returns rows, and NOT EXISTS then negates it
One row, P200 room 101, and it is correlated because the subquery names R.PROPERTY_ID and R.ROOM_NUM
Two rows, P100 room 101 and P200 room 101, because a room number can repeat across two properties
optionNotes: The subquery is re-run for each room and finds nothing for P200 room 101, which is precisely the room being hunted.
A correlated subquery cannot be evaluated once and reused, because its result changes with every outer row handed to it.
Leases cover P100 rooms 101 and 102 and P200 rooms 201 and 202, leaving P200 room 101 as the only room never leased.
P100 room 101 sits on lease L001, so it is excluded; both halves of the composite key are compared, exactly as they should be.
questions.takeaway: A subquery that names a column of the outer query is correlated: it runs once per outer row, which is what lets NOT EXISTS test each row on its own.

questions.scenarioTitle: Tracing the grain-free dry food back to a customer
questions.stem: To find who bought item CF21, a clerk writes `SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM IN (SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM FROM INVOICE WHERE INVOICE_NUM IN (SELECT INVOICE_NUM FROM INVOICE_LINE WHERE ITEM_ID = 'CF21'));`. CF21 appears on invoices 50710 and 50711, which belong to customers 1120 and 1420. What comes back?
options: Access Pet Center and Whiskers and Wags Boutique, the customers on the two invoices that include CF21
All three invoiced customers, because the innermost subquery returns more than one invoice number
Only Access Pet Center, because a subquery nested inside another subquery may return just one value
Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb, because the outermost SELECT reports whatever the innermost subquery matched
optionNotes: Read it inside out: two invoice numbers, then the two customer numbers on those invoices, then the two customer names.
Downtown Aquarium's invoice 50712 holds AV07 and FT88, so its customer number never reaches the outer condition.
IN is built for multi-row subqueries at every level; only a subquery compared with = has to return a single value.
The outermost SELECT reports CUSTOMER_NAME from CUSTOMER, and nothing from ITEM appears in the result at all.
questions.takeaway: Read nested subqueries from the inside out, and remember that IN accepts many values at every level of the nesting.

matchers.heading: Match each description to the term it defines
matchers.prompt: Five terms from Module 5 and eight descriptions taken straight from the KimTay and StayWell data. Click a description, then click the term that names it. Two cards list one table twice: when a card could fit more than one term, the more specific term is the answer.

cards.text: Writing FROM CUSTOMER C so the rest of the query can say C.BALANCE instead of CUSTOMER.BALANCE
cards.why: One table gets a short alternate name in the FROM clause, and that is all this term means.

cards.text: After FROM REP R, the name REP.LAST_NAME is rejected and R.LAST_NAME has to be used instead
cards.why: The new name replaces the table name for the rest of the query, which is a property only this term has.

cards.text: FROM REP R1, REP R2, so KimTay's one rep table acts as two tables and its rows can be compared with each other
cards.why: The same table is listed twice under two names so that two of its own rows can be compared; the aliases are just the mechanism.

cards.text: FROM CUSTOMER F, CUSTOMER S WHERE F.CITY = S.CITY AND F.CUSTOMER_NUM < S.CUSTOMER_NUM
cards.why: CUSTOMER appears on both sides of one join so it can be matched against itself to find two customers in one city.

cards.text: FROM REP, CUSTOMER with no condition linking them, which returns all 12 rep and customer combinations
cards.why: Every row of REP is paired with every row of CUSTOMER because nothing links the two tables.

cards.text: Pairing each KimTay customer with each StayWell student, which gives 16 rows out of 4 and 4
cards.why: Two unrelated tables in one FROM clause multiply, 4 times 4, instead of matching.

cards.text: SELECT CITY FROM REP and SELECT CITY FROM CUSTOMER: one column each, and both hold city text
cards.why: Same number of columns and the same kind of data, so the two results can be stacked with UNION.

cards.text: WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM INVOICE I WHERE I.CUSTOMER_NUM = C.CUSTOMER_NUM), run once per customer
cards.why: The inner query names a column of the outer row, so it cannot be evaluated once and reused.

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NAME, COUNT(*) FROM CUSTOMER C LEFT JOIN INVOICE I ON C.CUSTOMER_NUM = I.CUSTOMER_NUM GROUP BY C.CUSTOMER_NUM, C.CUSTOMER_NAME;
sqlChecks.expect: 4 rows, every count 1, including Companion Care Clinic - the COUNT(*) trap in review Q2

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT F.CUSTOMER_NAME AS FIRST_ONE, S.CUSTOMER_NAME AS SECOND_ONE, F.CITY FROM CUSTOMER F, CUSTOMER S WHERE F.CITY = S.CITY AND F.CUSTOMER_NUM < S.CUSTOMER_NUM;

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT CITY FROM REP UNION SELECT CITY FROM CUSTOMER ORDER BY CITY;
sqlChecks.expect: 3 rows: Brookville; Maple Grove; Northfield (m5-terms sandbox solution)

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER C WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM INVOICE I WHERE I.CUSTOMER_NUM = C.CUSTOMER_NUM);
sqlChecks.expect: 3 rows: Access Pet Center; Downtown Aquarium & Pets; Whiskers & Wags Boutique - Companion Care Clinic excluded (m5-terms sandbox solution and matcher card 8)

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT 'REP' AS TABLE_NAME, COUNT(*) AS ROW_COUNT FROM REP UNION ALL SELECT 'CUSTOMER', COUNT(*) FROM CUSTOMER UNION ALL SELECT 'INVOICE', COUNT(*) FROM INVOICE UNION ALL SELECT 'INVOICE_LINE', COUNT(*) FROM INVOICE_LINE UNION ALL SELECT 'ITEM', COUNT(*) FROM ITEM;

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT I.INVOICE_NUM, I.INVOICE_DATE, C.CUSTOMER_NAME, R.LAST_NAME FROM INVOICE I, CUSTOMER C, REP R WHERE I.CUSTOMER_NUM = C.CUSTOMER_NUM AND C.REP_NUM = R.REP_NUM ORDER BY I.INVOICE_NUM;
sqlChecks.expect: 3 rows: 50710 2026-06-14 Access Pet Center Kaiser; 50711 2026-06-14 Whiskers & Wags Boutique Perez; 50712 2026-06-15 Downtown Aquarium & Pets Hull (exercise 1)

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT DISTINCT T.DESCRIPTION FROM ITEM T, INVOICE_LINE L, INVOICE I, CUSTOMER C WHERE T.ITEM_ID = L.ITEM_ID AND L.INVOICE_NUM = I.INVOICE_NUM AND I.CUSTOMER_NUM = C.CUSTOMER_NUM AND C.REP_NUM = '20' ORDER BY T.DESCRIPTION;
sqlChecks.expect: 2 rows: Grain-Free Dry Food 30lb; Nylon Dog Leash 6ft (exercise 2)

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT T.DESCRIPTION FROM ITEM T, INVOICE_LINE L, INVOICE I, CUSTOMER C WHERE T.ITEM_ID = L.ITEM_ID AND L.INVOICE_NUM = I.INVOICE_NUM AND I.CUSTOMER_NUM = C.CUSTOMER_NUM AND C.REP_NUM = '20';
sqlChecks.expect: Also 2 rows without DISTINCT - rep 20's only invoiced customer (1120) has a single invoice, so DISTINCT collapses nothing on the shipped data. This is why exercise 2's prose presents DISTINCT as insurance rather than as a fix for duplicates that exist today.

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT S.LAST_NAME, S.FIRST_NAME, SUM(P.AMOUNT) AS PAID FROM STUDENT S LEFT JOIN LEASE L ON S.STUDENT_ID = L.STUDENT_ID LEFT JOIN PAYMENT P ON L.LEASE_ID = P.LEASE_ID GROUP BY S.STUDENT_ID, S.LAST_NAME, S.FIRST_NAME ORDER BY S.LAST_NAME;
sqlChecks.expect: 4 rows: Carter Miles 450; Ibrahim Layla 725; Nguyen Trang 1190; Park Jason NULL. The NULL is produced by the outer join, not stored in PAYMENT (exercise 3)

sqlChecks.expect: Still 4 rows, Park Jason NULL - an inner join to LEASE does NOT drop anyone, because every student has a lease. Only an inner join to PAYMENT drops Park, which is what exercise 3's hint must say.

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT S.LAST_NAME, SUM(P.AMOUNT) FROM STUDENT S LEFT JOIN LEASE L ON S.STUDENT_ID = L.STUDENT_ID JOIN PAYMENT P ON L.LEASE_ID = P.LEASE_ID GROUP BY S.STUDENT_ID ORDER BY S.LAST_NAME;
sqlChecks.expect: 3 rows: Carter 450; Ibrahim 725; Nguyen 1190 - Park Jason is gone. This is the exact failure exercise 3's hint diagnoses.

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT R.PROPERTY_ID, R.ROOM_NUM, R.ROOM_TYPE FROM ROOM R WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM LEASE L WHERE L.PROPERTY_ID = R.PROPERTY_ID AND L.ROOM_NUM = R.ROOM_NUM);
sqlChecks.expect: 1 row: P200 | 101 | Single (exercise 4, NOT EXISTS version - three columns)

sqlChecks.expect: 1 row: P200 | 101 (exercise 4, difference version - two columns only)

sqlChecks.expect: Error: SELECTs to the left and right of EXCEPT do not have the same number of result columns. LEASE has no ROOM_TYPE, so the difference version cannot report the room type - exercise 4's prose must say so instead of asking for the same three columns twice.

sqlChecks.expect: 1 row: Northfield (exercise 5)

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT R.LAST_NAME, C.CUSTOMER_NAME FROM REP R, CUSTOMER C;
sqlChecks.expect: 12 rows - the product of 3 reps and 4 customers (review Q1, matcher card 5)

sqlChecks.expect: 0 rows - every one of the five items has been ordered (review Q3)

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT CITY FROM REP UNION ALL SELECT CITY FROM CUSTOMER);
sqlChecks.expect: 1 row: 7 - UNION ALL keeps all 3 + 4 city values, versus 3 for UNION (review Q4)

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NAME, I.INVOICE_NUM FROM INVOICE I LEFT JOIN CUSTOMER C ON I.CUSTOMER_NUM = C.CUSTOMER_NUM;
sqlChecks.expect: 3 rows: Access Pet Center 50710; Whiskers & Wags Boutique 50711; Downtown Aquarium & Pets 50712 - Companion Care Clinic absent (review Q5)

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE BALANCE > ALL (SELECT BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20');
sqlChecks.expect: 1 row: Whiskers & Wags Boutique. SQLite rejects this statement with 'near "ALL": syntax error', so it is labelled MySQL only, kept out of every sandbox, and paired with the MAX rewrite (review Q6, summary engine note, m5-terms ALL row)

sqlChecks.expect: 3 rows: Access Pet Center; Downtown Aquarium & Pets; Whiskers & Wags Boutique. SQLite rejects this with a syntax error at the subquery after ANY, so it is labelled MySQL only and paired with the MIN rewrite (summary engine note, m5-terms ANY row)

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE BALANCE > (SELECT MAX(BALANCE) FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20');
sqlChecks.expect: 1 row: Whiskers & Wags Boutique - the runnable equivalent of > ALL (review Q6, summary engine note)

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, BALANCE FROM CUSTOMER WHERE BALANCE > (SELECT MIN(BALANCE) FROM CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = '20') ORDER BY BALANCE;
sqlChecks.expect: 3 rows in balance order: Downtown Aquarium & Pets 1200; Access Pet Center 3512.5; Whiskers & Wags Boutique 4820.75 (SQLite prints no trailing zeros) - the runnable equivalent of > ANY (summary engine note)

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT A.CUSTOMER_NAME, B.CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER A, CUSTOMER B WHERE A.CITY = B.CITY AND A.CUSTOMER_NUM <> B.CUSTOMER_NUM;

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME, LAST_NAME FROM REP, CUSTOMER WHERE REP_NUM = REP_NUM;
sqlChecks.expect: Error: ambiguous column name: REP_NUM (review Q8)

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT CUSTOMER_NAME FROM CUSTOMER WHERE CUSTOMER_NUM IN (SELECT CUSTOMER_NUM FROM INVOICE WHERE INVOICE_NUM IN (SELECT INVOICE_NUM FROM INVOICE_LINE WHERE ITEM_ID = 'CF21'));

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT CUSTOMER.CITY FROM CUSTOMER F;
sqlChecks.expect: Error: no such column: CUSTOMER.CITY - an alias replaces the table name (m5-terms closing paragraph)

sqlChecks.sql: SELECT REP.LAST_NAME FROM REP R;
sqlChecks.expect: Error: no such column: REP.LAST_NAME - the same rule stated on matcher card 2
